subtopic: ORDER OF THE HOUSE RESPECTING EXTENDED FRIDAY SITTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been certain consultations about the hours the house is to sit tomorrow. If there is general agreement perhaps we could have an order of the house stating that the house will sit for two hours tomorrow evening after private members hour. The order would be to the following effect: That if government orders Nos. 64, 75, 82 and 78 have not been disposed of earlier, after orders Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 4 relating to private bills have been disposed of, or at the end of the hour provided for private members business, whichever be earlier, the house will revert to government orders and continue to sit for two additional hours.
Perhaps that could be made an order of the house, Mr. Speaker, if hon. members are agreeable.

subtopic: ORDER OF THE HOUSE RESPECTING EXTENDED FRIDAY SITTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that for the balance of the session we are to dispense with private members hour, and consideration of private bills. When we return in the fall I understand that we are to consider notices of motions and motions for the production of papers in private members hour. Is not my understanding correct?

with regard to notices of motions and matters relating to papers being discussed in private members hour after the adjournment if the house sits then.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some weeks ago, that is to say on April 1, I mentioned to the house the several matters relating to the election law that require our attention. I made a suggestion at that time as to how we might proceed in dealing with those matters. Since then the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections has considered the possibility of introducing a system for the continuous or permanent listing of electors and on May 22 made a report on that particular matter. This means that the way is now clear for a review of the Canada Elections Act by the Standing Committee.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Hon. members know that upwards of 24 months are required between the time the act is amended extensively and the date of the writs for a general election. This means that we ought to begin the review of the act very

June 12, 1969
Business of the House
soon. One possibility is that the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections will decide to hold a series of meetings this September, during the summer adjournment of the house. In commenting on my suggestion of April 1, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) proposed that to save time the matter of election expenses should be separated out and sent to a special committee. I am quite prepared to agree to that proposal and therefore would be prepared to make a separate motion, if not this week, then next week, to make that reference to a special committee.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, it will be found that there will be general agreement to a motion to refer the Canada Elections Act, exclusive of the sections relating to election expenses, to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. If that expectation is correct, perhaps there could be an order to the following effect:
That the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections be empowered to study the Canada Elections Act, exclusive of sections 62 and 63, and to report to the house such proposals as the committee may deem advisable.
Perhaps if there is general consent that could be made an order of the house.

maintopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT-ORDER OF THE HOUSE FOR COMMITTEE STUDY, EXCLUSIVE OF ELECTION EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not necessary to spend much time commenting on the statement that the government house leader has made in connection with the subject of elections. Elections are a matter of great concern to all members of parliament. Indeed, in recent years some of us have had considerable experience. As a matter of fact I passed through my eighth election a year ago.
I am sure the more exposure we have to the electoral process, the more concerned we are about the great need for reform, particularly the need for carrying out more expeditiously electoral procedures.
Members of this party agree that the Canada Elections Act should be reviewed. As the government house leader has said, it is necessary to have a 24 month period between the completion of the electoral act reforms and the calling of another election. In view of the government's wavering performance, I am not sure whether we have sufficient time, but I would certainly approve of the suggestion that has been placed before this house, that this matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
[Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) .1
I also concur in the suggestion that the subject of election expenses be considered by a separate parliamentary group. We had a report on this subject a number of years ago and there is as much expedition required in this aspect of the electoral process as in the other matters which have been mentioned.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: CANADA ELECTIONS ACT-ORDER OF THE HOUSE FOR COMMITTEE STUDY, EXCLUSIVE OF ELECTION EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish simply to confirm that the statement made by the minister is in accordance with an understanding that we have. We are all agreed there is urgency in reforming the Canada Elections Act. Therefore we support the motion that it now be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
We are pleased that the government has accepted the suggestion that was made from this quarter, namely that the question of election expenses should be treated separately by a special parliamentary committee. We are glad to know that a motion to that effect will be made within a week, or indeed before we rise for the summer recess.
I want also to say that we approve of the proposal that one or both of these committees meet in September when the house is in recess. We support his proposal for two reasons. First, the subject matters being referred to these two committees are so important they must be dealt with when there is an opportunity to consider them adequately. Secondly, in view of the greater importance that we are now attaching to the work of committees, we believe this is a pattern that should be established. From time to time committees should meet when the house is not in session so they can devote their full time and attention to the important matters referred to them. We are happy to support the order proposed today by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald), and we look forward to supporting the other proposal when he moves it a few days from now.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity of participating in this debate on the second budget with which the house has been presented this session. While the budget introduced last Tuesday may be encouraging to some in that it does give some indication of fiscal management, it has been termed by others as discriminative, unrealistic and impractical. In short, it lacks a comprehensive approach to the basic issues which face this country-poverty, rising interest rates, the serious conditions in agriculture, and the
June 12. 1969

The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski continuance of high taxation which every year takes a greater portion of one's gross income.
There is growing reason to believe that the back of the Canadian taxpayer is nearing the breaking point, and that generally all taxpayers are thoroughly fed up by the demands of all levels of government. There is going to be a $250 million surplus, at the expense of the average taxpayer. This may be well and good, but where in this budget is any relief in sight for the average taxpayer? Where is there any positive aid for our aged, for those unfortunates on fixed pensions or incomes? Where is any positive measure to overcome the problems of housing, of regional disparity, to abate the ever-increasing prevalence of welfare and to relieve the ever-increasing crisis in agriculture?
I presume that the selective measures chosen by the minister are aimed at encouraging areas of slow growth. However, how will these areas be defined? What criterion will be used? Are we looking strictly at the large urban areas and overlooking the small rural centres which also deserve consideration? I hope not, but I am afraid that we are.
According to the budget the province of Alberta is a have province. This may be true so far as the cities of Edmonton and Calgary are concerned, but the rural areas of that province are a different matter. The tax penalty that the minister is proposing to levy on certain areas deserves an explanation from the minister, who is singling out cities like Edmonton and Calgary while allowing places like Montreal and Quebec City to go scot-free. It is particularly ironic in the case of Montreal, on whose behalf the minister decided to wipe out the Expo debt of $125 million. Why should Edmonton be slapped down for its initiative, its growth, its economic stability, its excellent labour picture and exciting future? The 22 centres in Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario that are suffering this injustice have just as many problems as the major centres in the other seven provinces, particularly when compared with Quebec which has a population almost four times that of Alberta.
If I may turn to the problems of rural Canada, particularly in western Canada, I should like to point out that with the continuing deterioration in the agricultural industry, which correspondingly has had an adverse effect on our rural towns, we are experiencing a mass migration into the cities of Edmonton and Calgary, a mass migration not of choice but of necessity. If some positive

measures are not instituted soon in these rural areas we will end up being a province of two cities. We already have more than one half of our people living in these two centres, and their population is increasing at a rapid pace.
This is one of my main reasons for rising to participate in this debate, to draw the attention of the minister and the government to the glaring omission of even token consideration of the present unprecedented crisis in western agriculture and the decline and abandonment of rural centres in the west. I am sorry to say that in this regard we do not seem to be getting too much assistance from the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand). It seems that most of the aid is going to eastern Canada and Quebec. We require some alternative employment to enable the people in the rural centres in my part of the country to earn a living. Certainly one would have thought that in this political era of participation and dialogue an imaginative and sensible program might have been brought forward to curtail the serious deterioration in the western farm economy. We expected that out of all the submissions and briefs presented, the task force reviews and conferences that have been held, some form of emergency relief would emerge.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
The wheat situation has not improved. Country elevators are full. Farm storage facilities are filled. There is no cash. The banks are commencing foreclosures on land and machinery. Finance companies are pressing for payments which were extended from last fall. There is a general climate of chaos and apprehension among the people of my area, many of whom are unable to meet their public utility bills. The most optimistic quota we can look forward to is five bushels for this crop year, the result being that most farmers will have to provide themselves with additional storage facilities for this fall's harvest.
Where will the money come from for this construction, Mr. Speaker? If conditions do not improve the majority of farmers will not be eligible for cash advances this fall because they will not have cleared their previous advances. They will not be marketing grain. As a result the provision of storage facilities will become a serious problem. I think the government should institute immediately a program of storage payments for farm stored grain or some alternative program in order to provide assistance for construction of storage
June 12, 1969	COMMONS
facilities. Better still, I think the government ought to get off its fat butt and market grain.
Another sore spot in the western farm economy is the present dairy policy and the administration of that policy. The establishment of minimum subsidy levels has imposed a severe hardship on many low income families on the prairies. We are told that this policy was instituted to encourage large, viable producers. That is a confirmed Liberal philosophy aimed at promoting bigness. I simply say this, Mr. Speaker. For years many of our small farmers depended on a few milk cows for groceries on the table and the necessary clothing for the children. By raising the minimum subsidy level the commission will not stop production by these farmers. They cannot stop producing; if they do, they will have to stop eating.
What is happening, one may ask? Many farmers, as a result of tough luck, a break in communication with the Canadian Dairy Commission or simple lack of knowledge, fall below the 420-pound level of production of butterfat in any given year and are disqualified as eligible producers. They cannot be re-established as eligible producers unless they buy a herd with a quota of 3,500 pounds. A herd of this size represents a sizeable investment in livestock, machinery and ancillary equipment vital to the operation. Furthermore, the majority of cream producers in western Canada are far below that level of production. So, as I say, our farmers must purchase herds with requisite quotas and transfer those quotas. The red tape encountered in transferring quotas is most frustrating; the results of applications are uncertain and this is a most questionable procedure. The red tape our farmers have to encounter in transferring quotas constitutes another form of discrimination.
And where are these quotas, the property of the Canadian Dairy Commission, being reallocated, Mr. Speaker-and please remember that the dairy commission has been created to assist farmers? Where else but in Quebec and Ontario. Those quotas have been given to the milk producers in those provinces. So we have the situation that in western Canada creameries are threatening to close because of decreased shipments while at the same time we are seeing a huge build-up of skim milk powder in Quebec and Ontario. And the closing of creameries is another severe blow to rural towns.
I am told that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) has been 29180-635
The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski trying desperately to market this skim milk powder at fire sale prices. He has failed in that field just as he has failed with wheat. Skim milk powder production has increased by 75 per cent since 1965 and each year the government is called on to purchase more of it. In 1967 the Canadian Dairy Commission purchased 101 million pounds and subsidized the private export of 53 million pounds. In 1968 the Canadian Dairy Commission purchased 200 million pounds of skim milk powder and subsidized the private export of 22 million pounds. It is clear that we have a total surplus of 222 million pounds. This government policy is being carried out while world stocks are at an all-time high. The result of that policy is that the Canadian Dairy Commission has lost about 15 cents per pound on sales. It has bought for 20 cents per pound and sold for 5 cents per pound on export markets.
In formulating present dairy policy the government has written off prairie cream producers. There can never be a clearer cut case of discrimination than we have here. I believe there is a place for the producer of farm separated cream in an equitable dairy policy. Furthermore, there is a place on the prairies for the dairy industry. I am sure that by discriminating against these producers the dairy commission will create more problems than it will solve in the over-all production of dairy products in Canada. By doing a little arithmetic one can easily calculate that the loss on skim milk powder is $33 million, and that figure does not take into account transportation and storage costs.
I strongly urge the dairy commission to look again at where its policy is leading us. If the program is designed to pacify producers in Quebec and Ontario, it is living up to its commitment. On the other hand, if that policy is designed to create a just society with equal opportunities for all, no matter whether they live in the maritimes, central or western Canada, one can only conclude that the policy is being abused. By utilizing the arts of gerrymandering, trickery and deception the government has created and is administering an invidious policy. I think it ought to be possible for anyone producing 300 pounds of butterfat to qualify for a subsidy and I think there is! merit in the idea of removing the minimum ceiling altogether. Present regulations make it impossible for a young farmer or small operator to go into business by buying a 3,500 pound production unit which may consist of about 15 cows plus machinery and housing. The Budget-Mr. Mazankowski involves major capital expenditures which many of our young farmers cannot afford.
Many prairie farmers today who are desperately searching for cash are selling five gallon cans of cream for $9.45. Those with subsidy quotas realize an average of $14.80 for the same quantity of cream. Is that fair, Mr. Speaker? I say it is definitely not fair. Nevertheless, when one needs food for the table and clothes for the children one tends to overlook this discouraging inequity and carry on producing.
In the light of existing conditions in the west and with the government giving us no consideration we often hear of western separation and alienation. One cannot be surprised to hear these things. This government's national policies and the Canadian Dairy Commission's policies are not helping to dispel this sort of talk.
About 700 farmers threatened, at a recent gathering in St. Paul, Alberta, to march on the nearest welfare office in search of financial assistance if their demands were not met. I was in touch with those farmers last week and was advised that neither the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) nor the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have as yet even acknowledged receipt of the brief that was sent. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we have not heard the last from this group. They are desperate, being the victims of poor weather, poor government and poor marketing policies. They are the victims of economic injustice brought about by lack of flexible government policies. Those policies control their destinies. They are the victims of misfortune. In providing or considering emergency assistance, the government is ignoring these people.
I now wish to comment about the price of beef. It is unfortunate that some are criticizing the farmer for the high price of beef. Beef is the only commodity at present which returns a fair price to the farmer.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am somewhat disturbed to hear the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) and other hon. members magnify the price of beef on the hoof. Yesterday, for example, choice steers were being sold in Calgary for $33 per hundredweight, a far cry from the $38 that has been publicized in the press and in this house.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Beef is $1.50 a pound at some markets.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The price of slaughtered beef recently reached a figure between $29 and $30. The increase of $3 per hundredweight represents a 10 per cent increase to the consumer and not the 25 per cent increase that has been publicized in some quarters. Meanwhile, meat prices in the stores have risen by 40 per cent.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I merely want to point out that the producer is not gaining in this spiral. It is the middleman somewhere along the way to the consumer who is taking advantage of the situation. I also point out that the figures I used are prices for choice steers. The majority sold for slaughter are medium to good and realize somewhere between $30 and $32 per hundredweight. I am sure I do not have to remind hon. members that when you walk into a store to purchase a steak there is only one price and that is based on choice quality. Steak is selling in the stores somewhere in the vicinity of $1.60 to $1.70 a pound. Why this spread? Who is raking off the profits? If this does not demand a full scale investigation, I do not know what does.
In all sincerity, I think the large food chains are attempting to shift the blame for the rising food costs on to the producer, but the real blame lies somewhere in between. This is completely irresponsible and I think the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) should clarify his position without hesitation.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has proposed a $2 acreage payment based on 1968-69 cultivated acreage up to a maximum of $2,000 for any farmer. I wholeheartedly support this recommendation and strongly urge the government to implement such a program immediately. It is estimated to cost between $150 million and $160 million. This is certainly not too high a price to pay for emergency relief to overcome the desperate plight on the prairies.
There is never a shortage of money for arts centres, airports, Canada Council grants or the C.B.C. What about the $80 million tariff write-off we have just been examining in the Public Accounts Committee, $75 million to one automobile manufacturer? There is always plenty of money for the ever-growing governmental bureaucracy.
It is interesting to note that in 1912 Canada had a population of seven million people with
June 12, 1969

20.000	federal employees. That is a ratio of one federal employee for every 350 citizens. Today, 60 years later, Canada's population has tripled to 21 million. However, the number of federal employees has increased by 2,500 per cent, almost to half a million, despite the advances in technology, computers and sophisticated administrative equipment. In other words, in 1912 we had one federal employee for every 350 Canadians and today we have one federal employee for every 40 Canadians. This is a shocking example of how bureaucracy grows with crippling socialistic schemes for the nation.
On April 18 I placed a question on the order paper regarding the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development which reads as follows:
What was the total number of people within the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, or its predecessor, who were directly concerned with the administration of Indian Affairs and services in the years 1965, 1966, 1967, 1968 and 1969?
The increase in staff has been 50 per cent since 1965. In 1965 there were approximately
1.000	people and in 1969 there were approximately 1,523, while the Indian population increased by less than 10 per cent in the corresponding period of time.
Looking at the 1968 Auditor General's report, we find further evidence of the ever-increasing administrative body. As it points out, in 1963 the cost of administrative overhead was $1 billion. This figure rose to $1,760 million for 1968-69, an increase of 76 per cent in six years. Increases in staff have occurred in 34 of the 42 departments-by some 10,629 people in the past year alone. The Auditor General further points to the continual rise in expenditures as a result of uneconomic and wasteful policies of the government. I refer to page 7 of the report of the Auditor General for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1968, wherein he states:
My report this year again directs the attention of the house to a number of expenditures that were uneconomical or wasteful. In my opinion more should be done to examine the underlying causes as to why so much of this kind of waste continues year after year.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will conclude by saying that now we have dispensed with some of the red herring issues such as abortion and homosexuality, and are soon to dispense with the official languages bill, I hope we can look forward to the government honestly facing the real problems which confront our country. We have heard a great deal from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and members of the government asking the opposition for their co-operation, suggestions, alternatives and ideas. Goodness knows, we have certainly been co-operative and have given them a lot of material and suggestions.
The real test of the Prime Minister's participatory democracy will come and will be proven only if he seriously considers some of our submissions and accepts some of the suggestions made by hon. members in this house. After all, we are the elected representatives of the people. We know the problems. We are in contact with these problems continuously. We are constantly in communication with our constituents. We do not need regional desks to solve these problems. What is needed is co-operation between the elected representatives of this distinguished house and the government of this country.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in this budget debate I intend to deal with three specific subjects. It has been my intention to deal strictly with the new ideas for regional economic expansion as they apply to my part of the country, northeastern Ontario, but since recent events in the Nigeria-Biafra conflict have underlined the seriousness of the situation and the danger to Canadians in that area, I wish to deal with it first.
I believe that the Department of External Affairs has never understood the situation in Nigeria and Biafra. In an attempt to appear neutral, Canada has actually taken sides. We cannot afford to align ourselves with one side or another in any struggle around the world. It is not for us to decide who is right or who is wrong. We can remain non-committed and still offer our help to alleviate the sufferings and difficulties arising from war.
What does Canada do? Whenever the department prepares a statement or an answer it refers to the Biafrans as "the rebels". This is automatically taking sides and it is also using a term which is inflammatory to the Biafrans. It is not up to us to say whether
10044	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. R. Stewart they are rebels. On other occasions the minister has intimated that the way to end the war is tor the Biafrans to surrender. No doubt it is, but to my mind that kind of statement on our part shows a complete lack of understanding of what is going on in that terrible struggle.
It has been my contention, and I still insist, that the two parties must come together at a conference table. Canada can help, and we must help. The department's answer repeatedly is that there is no lack of mediators, just a lack of agreement as to what negotiations should be pursued. This again shows a complete lack of appreciation of the problem. I suggest that there is a lack of the kind of mediators that would be acceptable to both sides. Canada is the only country that qualifies in this regard. Even the Emperor of Ethiopia was not successful in his kind efforts. We have underestimated ourselves. We are regarded as a big, powerful and influential country that is neutral, with no axe to grind, and has never had imperialistic tendencies or the desire to push anyone else around. This is the picture of Canada in the eyes of both Nigeria and Biafra.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
As far as a basis for negotiations is concerned, that is a contradiction in terms. The idea of getting together is for the purpose of negotiating. How can you have an agreement before you even get together to agree? It is up to us to put the proposal to both sides that they come together to talk on neutral ground, with Canada as the mediator. Let there be no preconditions other than a desire to talk. If one side or other refuses to go along with it, then there will be no one who can say that Canada did not at least try.
The recent shooting down of a Red Cross plane is something that cannot pass without mention. This is a matter which affects us seriously because we are involved in helping the Red Cross. It takes on even greater responsibility on our part because 12 Canadian crews are helping to fly relief supplies into Biafra and are in grave danger of their lives. My information is that a Red Cross plane was shot down by a Nigerian aircraft at 1855 hours on June 5, 50 kilometers southwest of Calabar, killing the crew of four. I am also informed that there is no question of it having been bright enough to see the Red Cross plane, and those of us who have seen those planes know that the large red cross on the tail and wings is unmistakeable.
[Mr. Stewart (Cochrane) .1
DEBATES	June 12, 1969
Whether or not this information is correct I cannot say because I do not have the actual documentation. The poor fellows are dead. But in any case the story is that it was certainly bright enough to see the airplane and the red crosses. The head of the Nigerian air force, Colonel Alad, is quoted as having said:
As far as we're concerned we are hitting at anything flying into Biafra, Red Cross or not.
One of the greatest organizations in the world today is Canairelief. They are a group of dedicated Canadians representative of various church organizations, and they have been saving countless lives by their efforts in the Nigeria-Biafra war. They have been doing so against great odds. But even our Department of External Affairs has not seen fit to help them in any way. Yes, we operate through the Red Cross-that is the argument of the government-but so do other countries, and those other countries also help the church organizations.
I go so far as to say that the department have a cavalier attitude toward Canairelief, considering them as a thorn in their side or a prick to their conscience. They say that they cannot recognize an organization bringing relief only to one side. This simply is not so because the church organizations are more active on the federal side of Nigeria than they are in Biafra. The airlift itself is only to Biafra because that is the area that is cut off.
It is time that the minister and his colleagues in the cabinet took a look at the whole policy regarding Nigeria-Biafra. It is time that the cabinet started making decisions on this subject instead of allowing the department to do so. It is the minister who has to take the responsibility in the department, and the cabinet should exercise its authority in formulating the policy.
I want to make it quite clear that the essential thing for Canada is not to take sides. There is no such thing as a one-sided responsibility in a struggle. No doubt both sides have done many things they should not do, but that is not for us to judge. However, I suggest that it is up to us to take the initiative to try to bring about an understanding so that this senseless war will end and so that lives will be saved.
The rectifying of disparities in various parts of Canada was one of the main aims of the government when it took office. We are all pleased that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) has introduced measures which will contribute in a
June 12, 1969	COMMONS
positive way to helping slow growth areas. My part of the country in northeastern Ontario is just such an area, but we are not of a breed that sits around waiting for the government to give us a handout. No, Mr. Speaker, we want to help ourselves, but we need orientation from governments.
Last weekend we held an economic conference in Cochrane and Kapuskasing which was successful beyond all predictions. When we first thought about having such a conference in northeastern Ontario we agreed that the problems of the area were so many and complex and so intertwined that it would not be sufficient to have representatives from only one sector of the economy. We agreed that we would have to have top representatives from various groups, from the financial and business community, and from government.
Most people in the southern parts of Canada do not understand the north. In order to attract the top kind of people to this conference I thought that the best way would be to have good representation from the government. So we decided we would ask two federal cabinet ministers to give one day each to the conference. That is how the whole thing began. Everyone knows that my counterpart in Cochrane at the provincial level is a minister in the provincial government, and together we decided we would be the cohosts of the economic conference.
It turned out that almost 100 businessmen from the southern part of Canada, from Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal, attended the conference. They are people who are leaders in the country's economy, people like the chairman of the board of the Montreal Trust Company, the vice-president of Metropolitan Life, the vice-president of Canada Life, the vice-president of Crown Life, the general manager of the Toronto-Dominion Bank, the executive vice-president of Imperial Oil, the vice-president of C.I.L., the president of Allstate-the list goes on and on. We had almost 100 people of that calibre.
These are people who are interested in the future development of the north. They came there without really knowing what they were coming to, but I can say that they went away very happy with what they had learned about northern Ontario. We discussed four main topics. We talked about capital investment. We talked about industry and natural resources. We spoke about tourism and transportation. Many of these things depend upon each other. You cannot talk about tourism in the north without talking about capital
The Budget-Mr. R. Stewart , investment, because money is needed to build tourist establishments. You cannot talk about industry in the north without talking about transportation, because people do not want to move industries to an area unless they are able to send their product out to market at a reasonable rate.
We discussed all of these topics in seminar form. For half of one day we gave these gentlemen the choice of three different things to do. After going to church they had an opportunity to take part in a fishing trip to see what the tourist possibilities were or they could take a flight in one of the provincial aircraft provided by my counterpart to look at the area and its natural resources from the air. The third choice was to look at some of the available industrial sites, particularly those having to do with the forest industry.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion attended on the first day of the conference. He spoke about the new regulations under the new legislation and of the idea of helping slow growth areas by means of incentives. On the second day the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) was with us in Kapuskasing,, and he spoke about the development of the north.
This kind of conference, which brings together such varied people, wakens people to what is available, shows them what the natural resources of an area are, and emphasizes the growth possibilities of the area. The people who attend such a conference try to come up with their own ideas on how to develop the area. This is precisely what happened in this case. In free periods when these gentlemen were discussing things among themselves they were making an honest effort to find ways and means of helping that part of the country.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
However, when the conference drew to a close my problem was how to know whether or not it had been a successful conference because these are busy men who have many problems. There was the possibility that they would go back to their offices, perhaps not think too much about what they had learned and let it remain in the back of their minds. But I can tell you that before they left the north some of these men came up with very good ideas concerning the betterment of northern Ontario which should be considered further. The representatives of one bank gave notice that they are changing some of their
10048	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. R. Stewart basic policies in respect of the north. An official of one of Canada's principal chemical companies told me one of their men would be employed full time in considering expansion in our part of the country. To my mind these are real results. Many of the results of this conference will not be seen perhaps for a number of years, but I believe this is an example of the way in which we should try to develop the underdeveloped areas of Canada. We should try to do this in concert with others and by amalgamating the efforts of government and industry. It is a mistake to sit back and ask the government to do everything. We must take the bull by the horns and do something ourselves.
I believe that the degree of federal and provincial co-operation was another great example of the success of the conference. The Minister of Lands and Forests of the province of Ontario and myself are not members of the same party, but that does not make any difference when it comes to the question of developing our area. We are both interested in the development of northern Ontario. It is only when the federal government and provincial governments work together in this way that we are able to really accomplish something. There was absolutely no question of political partisanship throughout this whole weekend. I think this will perhaps serve as an example of the co-operation we need.

Mr. Speaker, before concluding my remarks, I would like to add a few words on the official languages bill, particularly on the choice of the Commissioner of languages.
I have said it before, the Commissioner will have a very difficult task. He will have to have remarkable qualifications, be perfectly bilingual and understand the different mentalities of our country, and know exactly how others think.
Not only will he have to be a diplomat, possess a sound judgement and know how to hear grievances, but he will also have to be capable of judging problems according to the mentality of the people involved. Thus, it will be very difficult to find a man who is well qualified, to hold down that job.
In my opinion, the late Mr. Laurendeau would have been the right man for that position.
We will need an excellent Commissioner of languages, and I urge the government to choose him carefully. This choice should not be entrusted to the public service. I do not

DEBATES	June 12, 1969
want to criticize the public service but it is imperative that such a choice be made by the cabinet, and that it be well-advised.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the fourth budget this government has termed anti-inflationary which has been presented to the country during the past three years. The solution offered by the government in the first three was increased taxes. In order that we may decide how successful the policy of raising taxes has been I suggest we examine some of the figures of the consumer price index over the past few years because that will give us a good factual idea of just how this program of raising taxes has worked out for the country.
During the six years that the Conservative government was in power the average increase in the cost of living each year was 1.5 per cent.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How about unemployment?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then in 1964, the first year after the Liberal government took over, the cost of living rose 1.7 per cent. In 1965 it rose 2.5 per cent; in 1966 it rose 3.7 per cent; in 1967 it rose the same amount, 3.7 per cent; in 1968 it rose 4.1 per cent, and during the last 12 months it has risen 4.7 per cent. During the past 12 months the wholesale price index has risen 5.4 per cent. So I think we will agree it is very easy to decide that the policy which the government employed in the previous three budgets has been a complete failure so far as slowing down the steady increase which was taking place in the cost of living is concerned, because that increase had accelerated each year.
After each of these budgets during the past three years I and other members of the opposition have suggested two means of controlling the steadily increasing rise in the cost of living. These two methods are completely different from the method of raising taxes. The first method is by controlling government spending which has doubled during the past six years that the Liberal government has been in power. It has increased from $6| billion to $13 billion. Action must be taken to relieve the upward pressure of prices brought about by the steadily increasing government spending which has taken place year after year. The government's answer on each of these occasions was that it could not make
June 12, 1969

cuts in the current fiscal year. Of course, as we know, during the next fiscal year the cuts that were made were purely routine.
Any member of parliament who has been a member of a government knows that each minister in charge of each department inflates his estimates to the highest possible point before he presents them to the Treasury Board because he knows they will be slashed very materially. He knows that the more he has in his estimates the better chance he will have of coming out of this very trying experience with something of a reasonable nature with which to operate his department during the next 12 months. The President of the Treasury Board takes great pleasure each year in cutting down materially the estimates of each department. The net result is he is pleased and the minister is pleased because they usually end up where they had hoped to end up. That is what goes on each year when the Minister of Finance says he plans to cut the next year's estimates materially. The cut is a routine matter. It really is nothing that has not been taking place in parliament for the last 100 years.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Let us ask ourselves whether it is possible to make important cuts during the present fiscal year. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and his predecessor have said during the past three years that this is not possible to do, but is it possible? In 1962 the Conservative government was faced with an international payments problem, but at that time it showed that this could be done. On June 23, 1962, we made the decision to reduce current expenditures by no less than $200 million in that fiscal year. This means that that cut was made at the rate of $265 million for a full fiscal year. That cut was accomplished during a period of only three days. We showed that it could be done.
The second proposition we put forward was to control the cost of living by bringing about lower prices through an increase in productivity. We urged the government to introduce incentives which would induce industrialists to instal new plant,, machinery and industrial systems to make it possible to manufacture at lower cost, thereby lowering the selling price. Once again the Minister of Finance and his predecessor scoffed at this idea and would take no action to introduce the necessary incentives to make it possible to improve the productivity of this country. So during the past three years we have had, as I pointed out by citing figures from the consumer price
The Budget-Mr. Hees
index, a state of escalation in the rate of the increase in the cost of living, year by year. This demonstrates more clearly than any words I or anyone else might say the complete failure of the government's policy of increasing taxes in the past three budgets.
We now have another budget. Let us have a look at it. It offers two new approaches. The first is to control the cost of living by deferment of construction in cities over 50,000 in the three provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta, by withholding the capital cost allowance of 5 per cent in the next two years. The second plan is to complete the Kennedy Round tariff reductions immediately instead of waiting for the next three years over which the planned reduction had been worked out with industry. It is now up to us in discussing this budget to decide whether these two plans will work any better than the previous plan put forward by the government to increase taxation.
Let us first examine the plan to delay construction in cities over 50,000 population in Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta. We know that building costs are going up 12 per cent per year. If a builder in any of these centres defers construction during the next two years, as the government hopes they will, he will know perfectly well that when he commences construction two years from now he will in all probability be faced with construction costs 24 per cent higher than they are today. It is obvious that no builder is going to defer construction for two years and absorb that kind of an increase in cost. In every case builders will simply absorb the 5 per cent capital cost allowance in their not insignificant profit and go ahead and build. Any businessman in the country can tell you that this is a fact. There is no doubt about it.
Let us now have a look at the effect of immediate tariff cuts in respect of the Kennedy Round instead of over the next three years. There is no machinery available in peacetime to require importers to pass along to consumers the benefits they receive as a result of these lower import duties.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) has stated that he is considering the setting up of machinery to pass along these savings to the consumer. He referred to the sales tax on drugs that was removed. The minister knows perfectly well that when the sales tax on drugs was removed the government found there was no way by which it could require druggists to pass on the savings to the consumer, and that

June 12, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Hees
in very few cases were these savings passed on.
When the minister talks about setting up machinery to require importers to pass on these tax reductions to the consumer he is simply misleading the public because he knows perfectly well that in peacetime there is no way he can do this which will be effective. We may find out that in a few cases importers will pass on their savings because of their good nature or good will, or because they are faced with a very competitive situation, but these cases will be very few and far between. In the vast majority of cases these tariff reductions will simply be absorbed by importers in their profits through the price of goods. The costs will not be affected in this way and will not be reduced. They will continue to rise as they have during the past three years. We can therefore only conclude, that this budget, like its three predecessors, is going to be a failure. As they say in show-business, it looks like the minister has got another flop on his hands.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member-

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will be glad to answer the minister when I finish. I only have five more minutes at my disposal, but I would be very glad to answer any questions he wants to put at that time. I hope he understands that I take this attitude only because I have a very short time left.
As they say in the automobile industry, it looks like the minister produced an Edsel. In fact, I understand that in the cabinet they have now stopped calling him Edgar; he is now called "Edsel" by his colleagues.
Let us be constructive and decide what the government should do. First of all I suggest it should do three things. It should reduce government spending at this moment, in the present fiscal year, by $250 million, thereby taking the pressure off prices and thereby slow down the increase in the cost of living.
As I pointed out, the Conservative party showed in 1962 that this could be done. If seven years ago we could reduce expenditures by $200 million in one fiscal year without any trouble at all, the present government should be able to reduce expenditures today by $250 million, particularly in view of the inflation that has taken place during the seven intervening years. There is no question but that this can be done. It must be done to take the pressure off prices by removing this very large upward drive on prices throughout

the country. This is being caused by the increase in government expenditure.
The second thing the government must do is increase productivity in this country and reduce the cost of goods. This can be done by lowering the cost of production. As I have pointed out, the only way this can be brought about is by introducing tax incentives which will induce producers across the country to instal new machinery, plant and production systems, which will in turn enable them to produce more efficiently, bring their costs down, and sell their goods to the Canadian public at more reasonable prices.
The third thing I propose that this government should do is to substantially eliminate the waste which is taking place today. This can be done by the establishment of better economic co-ordination and planning. We should establish an economic planning committee composed of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), with the chairman being the Minister of Finance.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Any top civil servant in our economic departments will tell you privately-and those of us who have been in government know them all very well indeed-that tremendous waste is taking place today in the government through duplication and overlapping in our major economic departments. Sometimes five different departments are doing the same kind of thing. By centralizing under an economic planning operation the sinews of these five economic departments, under the able chairmanship of the Minister of Finance, I feel sure that a great deal of this waste can be cut out. Such a committee could make possible the kind of action which the former deputy prime minister, when he resigned a few weeks ago, said this government is unwilling to take. I refer, for instance, to controlling inflation, producing housing which people can afford to buy, and a program that will deal effectively with pollution.
Such an economic planning committee could make possible the kind of program brought forward by the government of Australia in the realm of housing, something which we in this country need desperately. There, through the work of a committee of this kind, it has been possible to produce
June 12, 1969	COMMONS
three-bedroom houses for $12,000 apiece, with a down payment of $1,200 and a mortgage of 5 per cent. That is the kind of action Canada needs today. But this government, as the former deputy prime minister said at the time of his resignation-and he ought to know, if anybody does-refuses to move because of the classroom attitude of the Prime Minister, who would far sooner deal with constitutional matters and does not give a hoot about the practical problems facing the ordinary citizens of Canada, the kind of problems I have just mentioned.
This government obviously thinks it has three years in office before the next election takes place. It shows no inclination to do anything but take things very, very easy. Therefore we see, just one year after the last election, that a government about which the people of Canada had great expectations when it came into office has turned out to be simply a government of false expectations. I say to the government that there is a great deal to be done, as the former deputy prime minister said very eloquently when he resigned. He pointed out the great weaknesses existing in the government. All the ministers, led by the Prime Minister, are responsible for this lethargy and unwillingness to tackle anything other than constitutional and theoretical problems; they are unwilling to turn their attention to the problems the people of Canada want solved.
There is a big job to be done. The next three years will pass faster than the government imagines. I ask the government to get on with the job it was elected to do and to show the people of Canada that it is a government and not simply a group that wants to sit down and ride out its time.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question that is in several parts? I am sure he wants to be very fair in his assumptions and that he read the budget speech before making such a presentation. This is the kind of response Ministers of Finance have given to every one of our speeches on the budget during the past three years. Mr. Speaker, under the new system in parliament our committees are doing a great deal of very constructive work, but I feel they are not receiving the recognition they deserve in the House of Commons. I believe that reports submitted to the house by standing committees should be given more publicity. I should first of all like to compliment the members who served on the Standing Committee on
June 12, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Hopkins National Resources and Public Works for the work they have done over the past months. I think it is important for the image of this committee to point out that not once did we have to cancel a meeting for lack of a quorum. I believe this is a very definite tribute to the members who served on that committee. In order to give their work some publicity I shall read from the fourth report of the committee so it will be on the record of the house:
Your committee recommends that as soon as possible the government allocate more money for scientific research projects that are now under way, as well as to continue new programs for the future.
During the study of the estimates of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, the committee learned that more and more funds from that company's regular budget will be required to continue the operations of several nuclear power generators until such time as private enterprise is financially capable of taking them over, probably about 1978. In the meantime, these established expenses will be a drain from the research funds of the company and these should be supplemented.
Canada has been in the forefront in nuclear research in the world with emphasis on the peaceful role of atomic energy and your committee recommends that increased financial support be given to research projects in this field.
The committee commends the government on the establishment of the Inland Waters Centre at Burlington and the work being carried out there on water pollution research. We recommend that this be given full and increased assistance and that other complementary centres be set up where needed.
Your committee is concerned by the increasing magnitude of air, water and soil pollution and the jurisdictional conflict which hampers the finding and implementing of proper solutions.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Your committee recommends that the government draft a code of standards for the cleaning up of and the future protection of all Canadian waters; that provincial approval of such a code be sought; and that the federal government provide an enforcement procedure-if necessary by means of an amendment to the Criminal Code.
Your committee also recommends that a centre or centres similar to the Canada Centre for Inland Waters be set up to centralize all existing and future federal research in air and soil pollution and to extend and speed up such research so that codes of standards may be drafted to protect the air and soil from pollution.
During its study of the estimates of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, your committee was informed that there would not be any "Canadian produced" heavy water available in Canada this year. Your committee recommends therefore that the words "Canadian produced" be deleted from Vote L20 thus enabling the company to purchase heavy water from non-Canadian sources.
The committee wishes to state that it has been greatly impressed by the contributions from the Canadian science community and commends all

personnel involved in scientific progress in Canada on their achievements.
Your committee commends these estimates to the house.
I should like to say a word on the political activities of employees of Crown corporations. I am given to understand that in the past the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority had one employee at least who ran as a federal member of parliament in either 1962 or 1963, and I believe the Polymer Corporation had one employee who contested two elections. But there are some Crown corporations in Canada whose employees are not permitted to participate in political activity or party politics. I think that some uniform plan should be worked out in this regard because in the case of Crown corporations, which are run in much the same way as a private enterprise with people working as carpenters, tradesmen of various types and general labourers, I do not think it is fair to refuse employees the opportunity of participating in the activities of the political party of their choice. I ask that this matter be looked into.
We have a very useful fund in the Department of Transport for the construction and improvement of airports. Money in this fund is allotted on the basis of $1 million per annum, which is quite inadequate to look after these needs in communities across Canada today. At the present time all these funds are committed for 1969 and there is very little left in the 1970 budget. In my riding, in and around the towns of Pembroke, Petawawa and Deep River, we have started the construction of an airport which is already one of the most used airports along the new route that was started by Royalair from Montreal. The route starts in Montreal and goes on to Ottawa, Pembroke, Peterborough, Toronto and St. Catharine's, with other lines added since. However, the airport at Pembroke is the only one along the entire route that is not paved. It supplies 50 per cent of the passengers on the entire run. It is used extensively by the scientists from Atomic Energy of Canada Limited at Chalk River and by the Department of National Defence at Petawawa.
I will give hon. members some examples of aircraft movements at the airport in Pembroke over a period of four months. In December of last year there were 461 aircraft movements, and in another month there were 1,325. In still another month there were 1,878 aircraft movements at this unpaved airport, and in yet another month 2,489 on what is a sod runway. So I appeal to the Department of Transport and to the Treasury Board to have
June 12, 1969	COMMONS
this airstrip paved at the earliest possible time.
In another area, the town of Mattawa is looking forward to the development of an airstrip there. As |you know, I am privileged in having a very beautiful riding which covers 64 townships and several organized villages and municipalities. Sometimes I wish I had an aircraft or a helicopter, but if an airstrip were built in the vicinity of Mattawa a very good tourist trade could be developed. Also, fishermen could fly in and out of the area, and so could hunters. Another important point is that if there were an airstrip at Mattawa a dentist could come into that community of 3,000 people for one day a week. Otherwise, the community does not have these services because of the lack of modern conveniences.
Over the past few years the Department of Public Works has had a very useful program called the tourist wharf policy. Under this policy wharves and docks up to a value of $15,000 are built on waterways. They are paid for by the Department of Public Works. There has been some talk from time to time that this program might be cancelled. I have heard this for the last few years, but I am glad to say that this decision has not been made because approximately only $200,000 a year is made available for this program. It provides a service to communities which normally would not have it because these docks and wharves are built in municipalities that are usually not wealthy, and we all know that every municipality today is under a heavy taxation burden at the local level. This is a very useful program which brings tourists into the area. It helps to promote the tourist trade and it promotes healthy recreation. I think it would be a very serious error if this program were ever dropped by the Department of Public Works.
As a matter of fact, it seems to me that $200,000 is far too little for such an important program which will enrich the lives of so many people as well as the lives of those who come to visit the area. I feel that not only should the fund not be cancelled but that the amount should be doubled. This is not something that has cost a lot of money. Much good can be done in many places with a small sum of money compared with some other projects.
Coming as I do from the upper Ottawa valley, an industry that is of crucial importance to me and to many people in my area is the forest industry. In our area 3,200 people make their living from the timber resources of Algonquin Park, and all this propaganda 29180-636J
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins that is coming over the airwaves about the slaughter of our natural resources is just so much talk for the record. In this regard one matter that has not been pointed out is that this spring many of the companies who have operations in the park planted 300,000 trees apiece. The trees were provided by the Department of Lands and Forests, but the companies paid the wages of those who planted them.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
An attempt has been made to implant the idea that once you cut down our forests nothing is left. This is far, far from the truth. As we all know the forest is a renewable resource. We also know that the people who depend upon the forest and its products for their livelihood are not going recklessly to destroy that from which they make their living. I think that is a point that should be made very strongly.
I think the point should be equally strongly made in favour of the forest industry that the forestry research station at Chalk River is cultivating trees that grow three to four times as fast as natural growth. In artificial conditions under lights a birch tree has been grown to the height of 13 or 14 feet in one year. These trees are exposed to lights and other treatment for 24 hours a day. I say these conditions are artificial because they are completely foreign to the world of nature, but this does give some idea of the kind of experiment being carried on.
The forest industry in the Algonquin Park area also supplies wood to the furniture industry in southern Ontario which employs
10,000	workers. I make that point to show that my area is not the only one to benefit from the forest industry. I hope I will have other opportunities to put other important facts on record, but I think the important thing to note is that the forest is a renewable resource.
I do not agree for one moment with 34 townships being set aside for the operations of an organization such as the Wild Lands League which claims a little over 800 members. The city of Toronto could be placed several times over within the area of Algonquin Park. There is an area already set aside for the Wild Lands League. Our attitude is that we are willing to live and let live, but we believe in the multiple use of this area.
Another important matter I want to mention is of an historical nature. On a high hill across the Ottawa River from the town of
June 12, 1989

The Budget-Mr. Hopkins Mattawa stood a cross that was placed there by Champlain. Time and again it has fallen down and been replaced, but for at least the last year the cross has not stood. I should like to suggest to the Department of Indians Affairs and Northern Development that the historic sites board adopt this place as an historic site and place the cross there as a permanent remembrance of the days when Champlain travelled up the Ottawa River. Many people in the past have watched for this cross as they have driven along highway 17 through Mattawa, and now it is no longer there. Therefore I recommend to the historic sites board some action along the line I have suggested.
In the government shuffle to bring constructive economies into our financial affairs I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) on the first major balanced budget, with a forecast surplus, in many years. However, I hope that in this shuffle the new military hospital planned for Base Petawawa does not get lost, because the hospital is very badly needed. I hope the colleagues of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) in Treasury Board will be very kind to him in this regard.
I should like to conclude on this note. Since certain pressure groups, such as the Wild Lands League, are putting pressure on the Ontario government to change the regulations in Algonquin Park, and throw out industry altogether, as would be the case if the league had its way, I think we should also think of all the asphalt and concrete that is being thrown over the best soil of many parts of Canada. For example, in the Niagara peninsula concrete buildings are being constructed and asphalt laid every day on good, fruit producing soil. Therefore I suggest it is not the forest industry of Canada that we should be concerned about. As I have said, the forest is a renewable resource, but that is not the case when you cover the best soil in the country with concrete buildings.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks may I read the amendment proposed by my party. It is relevant to the remarks I am about to make. The amendment reads as follows:
"regrets the continuing inability of the Government to curb the relentless increase in the cost of living since 1965, while increasing the hardship on the unemployed, the poor, pensioners, farmers, and other victims of the just society'.
I will not, as did the hon. member who just resumed his seat, congratulate the minister on his balanced budget. The technicalities of budget balancing mean precious little to the poor of this country, to the unemployed and to the regionally disadvantaged. I commend that comment to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and his colleagues in parliament.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, the most urgent problem facing Canada today is poverty- ugly poverty, poverty that is real throughout this country, poverty that is all too prevalent throughout this country. This problem is not unique to Canada. That great, affluent society, the United States, is equally concerned about the paradox of poverty in the midst of plenty. That question, too, is gnawing at the conscience of the United States. As in Canada, poverty can be found almost everywhere in the United States. It is found not only in the steaming ghettos of the eastern cities but also
June 12, 1969	COMMONS
in the ramshackled countryside of Appalachia. The same can be said of Canada.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, what are we doing about poverty in Canada? What are we doing to help the poor of this country? Perhaps we might ask ourselves this question. Who are the poor people of Canada? The obvious answer is that the poor are those who are poor by material standards. The poor are the regionally disadvantaged people. The poor are those who live in poverty on the reservations of Canada or in the slums of our big cities. The fact is that we have poverty in Canada. Our poverty recently was defined by the Economic Council of Canada and according to that definition we have an abundance of poverty.
I realize that what I am about to read has been quoted many times before, Mr. Speaker. Nevertheless, what has been read before bears repeating. I shall repeat it in the hope that someone in the government of this country may hear me and become seized of the fact that the real problem facing this country today is poverty. Perhaps something will be done about it. May I therefore read part of the sixth chapter of the fifth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada:
Poverty in Canada is real. Its numbers are not in the thousands, but the millions. There is more of it than our society can tolerate, more than our economy can afford, and far more than existing measures and efforts can cope with. Its persistence, at a time when the bulk of Canadians enjoy one of the highest standards of living in the world, is a disgrace.
What is poverty in Canada? Those who have seen it, felt it, experienced it-whether as its victims or as those trying to do something about it-can supply some telling descriptions.
The report of the Economic Council states that any man earning less than $3,000 a year and supporting a wife and child in living below the poverty line. Commenting on the report of the Economic Council the Globe and Mail had this to say in part in an editorial of September 30, 1968:
The average Canadian does not need the council to tell him that it is impossible for a family of three to live with anything remotely approaching dignity on $2,641.60 a year: his own budget tells him so. A family might do it without going hungry if it lived in a Newfoundland village where the fish were plentiful and free, but not in any of the built-up parts of Canada where most of our people live. Yet, as the council pointed out with anger, more than a quarter of our non-farm population is forced to live in this appalling poverty.
Again I ask, what will we do about poverty in this country? There are two types of poor people in this country. Some are unable to
The Budget-Mr. McGrath sustain themselves because of physical hand icaps or circumstances over which they have no control. These people must depend on the charity of the state. They depend on welfare and its concommitant degradation. Nevertheless, we must be concerned about a larger group. The people in that group through no fault of their own are poor because they have inadequate incomes or because they suffer from chronic unemployment. I refer to the regionally disadvantaged people of Canada.
I come from a province that is considered regionally disadvantaged. A few weeks ago I was at an Indian reservation in Manitoba and saw appalling poverty. The people of the reservation could also be described as regionally disadvantaged. These, then, are the poor people of this country. They live in its various regions. Unfortunately, many of our poor also live in large cities.
To illustrate the point I am making about regionally disadvantaged people I wish to refer to a report of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics which shows that a fisherman working in the fishing industry of Newfoundland in February or March of this year received on the average $62 after working a 44.8 hour week. His counterpart in British Columbia who does the same work earns almost $84 after working a 30.6 hour week. That, Mr. Speaker, is regional disparity. That sort of thing, I hope, is being considered at the dominion-provincial conference being conducted at this time. The example I have cited, and I make no apology for saying this, is a glaring example of how working men are exploited in the regionally disadvantaged areas of this country. A man working 45 hours a week in a fish plant and earning $60 is at least working, able to hold his head up and does not have to lose his dignity or pride by being forced to appeal to the state for public welfare. Granted his plight is a serious one because of runaway inflation and rising prices, but at least he is able to work. Although I am concerned about him, I am more concerned about the man who does not have a job.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I am also concerned about the man working in the cities of my province

where we have a guaranteed minimum wage of $1 an hour for men and 70 cents an hour for women. I have in my hand a pay cheque of one of my constituents living in St. John's. His pay envelope covers a 46-hour week. The hourly rate of pay is $1.15 and his gross earnings are
10054	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. McGrath $52.90. From that $52.90 he must pay $1.70 in income tax, which is a crying shame.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That man should not have to pay income tax. It the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) were here, I would refer him and other members to the amendment the other night of the New Democratic party which, unfortunately, the government did not accept. This man had to pay 65 cents unemployment insurance and 74 cents for the Canada Pension Plan. His total deductions from his $52.90 for the 46-hour week were $3.09, giving him a net take-home pay of $49.81.
The man to whom I am referring has a wife and child to support. He lives in a basement apartment for which he pays $115 a month. He cannot afford to buy steak. He cannot even afford hamburger. He cannot even afford to live, yet he is a working man. He has to pay $115 a month rent because the state has failed to provide adequate public housing. He is forced to live in a damp basement because the province in which he lives and the federal government are unable to get together to provide him with public housing.
That is the crime of poverty in this nation today. That is what is crying out for justice in this country today. The paradox of Canada is the growing gap between the rich and the poor, with the rich getting richer and the poor getting poorer. I make no apology for using that hackneyed phrase because they are the only words I can muster to describe the situation.
I have seen poverty in other areas of Canada but I am more familiar with the poverty in my own city and constituency. We have the largest families and the lowest per capita income in Canada. We have the highest per capita cost of living in Canada. I offer that as a paradox in terms of the human tragedy it represents. This gap is widening in my city, province and throughout the country. You do not have to travel 1,500 miles to St. John's, Newfoundland to find this poverty. I suggest you can find it right here in the city of Ottawa. You will certainly find it in abundance in the cities of Montreal and Toronto. This is the tragedy of our time. This is the real problem in Canada today, not bilingualism or biculturalism but the bread and butter issue of abject poverty that is all around us.
We have lived through the Pearson era when, coincidental with the Kennedy

DEBATES	June 12, 1969
administration, the liberals said they were going to tackle this problem. They declared war on poverty. That war on poverty has been shelved in the dusty archives of hackneyed political campaign phrases, perhaps to be dusted off and taken out in a few years' time to be used in some subsequent election. In the last election campaign we had the era of the just society, a phrase which is becoming more and more meaningless as the weeks go by. Perhaps that phrase too will end up in the dusty archives of used political campaign slogans to be taken out at some opportune time and used again. What satisfaction does that give to my poor little friend in St. John's, Newfoundland, who takes home $49.81 for working 46 hours from which he must feed his wife and child and pay $115 a month rent because this government has failed to provide him with public housing? It is precious little consolation, Mr. Speaker.
We have reached the point in this country when we must do more than just talk about poverty. We must do more than try to epitomize the problem in fancy phrases. We must have a realistic program to attack it. I do not know what is going on behind the closed, doors at the federal-provincial conference. I know there is not a great deal going on in this house today. One only needs to look around to see the evidence. Perhaps someone may hear what I am saying, and perhaps it may even filter through the secure doors of that building where the conference is taking place. Perhaps then these men who have the responsibility of heading the provincial and federal governments will come to grips with the serious problem of poverty.
The Canadian Council of Churches and the Canadian Catholic Conference recently issued a paper as a consequence of a study of poverty in Canada. Perhaps hon. members will bear with me if I quote from the June, 1969 issue of Canadian Churchman.
The resulting report notes that people today are in a hurry to be fully alive, free from daily want, sharing social power and a better life. "The deprived are saying to the privileged, 'Damn your charity. Give us justice.' Those in need are impatient because there is no longer any valid excuse for injustice and discrimination. Abundant resources and technical know-how can provide necessities and opportunities for all-given enough moral will and political courage."
The just society is still a dream, notes the report. The gap is still widening between rich and poor nations and the rich and poor within nations.
"The reality is a disgrace, which sees 4,000,000 to 5,000,000 Canadians enslaved by economic and social want. Public priorities still put the power of money before the needs of people."
June 12, 1969	COMMONS
1 have been in this house since the beginning of this session. I have listened to debates on satellites, defence budgets and everything else, but I have yet to hear a concrete proposal emanating from the government to come to grips with the real problem of this nation, the problem of poverty. It is just a few months since the Economic Council of Canada in its fifth annual report dealt extensively with this problem and defined it for all to see, except those who have not the eyes to see, and I suggest that surely the government of Canada falls into that category. On behalf of the poor of this country I can only re-echo to the empty treasury benches what the Christian churches of this country have said: "Damn your charity. Give us justice."
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
