speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the study of a budget is a kind of self-examination for a government. It is also an opportunity for hon. members to make suggestions and, as it were, to examine the economic health of the country. I would like to restrict my remarks to a particular aspect of the Canadian economy.
Before getting into my topic, I would like to say to the hon. member who spoke before me that I share several of his opinions, except that I think it is an easy solution to leave it to the federal government to settle the problems.
I would like to remind him that the problems he mentioned a while ago, mainly that of poverty, will only be settled when the three government levels have arrived at a fair distribution of responsibilities as well as of the resources that will enable them to assume those responsibilities.
Before I deal with two subjects close to my heart, such as the present depression in the textile industry-which is of concern to my constituency, as it gives some 2,200 jobs to my constituents-I must say that I attended at lunch time a study meeting of the Canadian Textiles Institute, and after having heard their grievances, I came very close to elaborating on this matter.
Unfortunately, I believe that any aspect of the Canadian economy is as urgent or even more generalized, and I want my remarks to be a kind of SOS from Canadian municipalities, in the present economic context.
In the present government trilogy, there is no doubt at all that the municipal level is treated as a poor retarded child. That
The Budget-Mr. Mongrain reminds me, Mr. Speaker, of a baby who would hide under the table while two older children are quarrelling for a cake and who could only have a few crumbs falling from the table during that quarrel.
I am bringing this matter up for another reason. It is because this afternoon and tomorrow the premiers of the ten provinces are gathered here in Ottawa. They are mainly responsible for that lack of dialogue between municipal, provincial and federal authorities.
I would like to avoid, as much as possible, any partisan consideration and discuss the matter as objectively as possible and put the blame, if need be as fairly as possible. But to prove clearly that I agree with the leader of the government and the country, I would like to quote a few words which he said at the opening of the convention of the Canada Federation of Mayors which was held in Ottawa last week.
After having recalled that urbanization in Canada is being carried on at a very fast pace, with the result that in the year 2,000, it is expected that at least 50 per cent of Canadians will be living in large urban areas, which are already a source of unimaginably acute problems, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) added:
We cannot expect one single level of government to satisfy all those requirements. There has always been and there will always be numerous aspects of urban renewal that must be left to local initiatives, to local preferences and to local administration exclusively.
That is the municipal government.
As far as others are concerned, it is preferable that the provinces deal with them at the regional level. Finally, there are still other aspects which represent questions with which the Parliament of Canada must necessarily be concerned.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime minister is absolutely right. We should grant the municipal representatives the right to attend constitutional conferences, particularly those where division of taxation is discussed, because municipal governments are nearer to the people, as well as the oldest form of government. It is only fairly recently that they became creatures of the provinces. The municipal government has both feet on its home ground and is closest to the people. Every day, it hears their grievances and their requests. The spokesmen of the municipal government should be invited to take part in the dialogue,
1005S
June 12, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Mongrain to outline their views and to find solutions to problems.
And the Prime Minister added:
If the federal and provincial governments have decided to proceed with the complete revision of the constitution, the reason is that we are now faced with many constitutional provisions which were drafted according to what were the realities in 1867. The few provisions dealing with the municipal organization of the country have not yet been dealt with during that revision; but the next intergovernmental meeting which will take place in June will be partly devoted to various aspects of our constitutional law, like the spending power of the federal government, which closely affects municipal governments.
Mr. Speaker, I am still amazed that the spokesman for the municipal governments have not been invited to participate at least as observers, in those discussions when their fate is at stake.
And I quote further:
I suggest the future stages of this constitutional review could very well involve a comprehensive study of the municipalities' role in a federal state.
I welcome that suggestion. The Prime Minister added:
The new tendencies that I have tried to describe to you this morning raise a whole series of pertinent questions each of which warrants a detailed study and a full debate; I shall quote only three of them. First, the physical presence of the federal administration in a great number of municipalities, under the form of airports, harbours, railways, and a whole range of government agencies and public undertakings; how can we make sure that this more and more keenly felt presence and its socio-economic effects will contribute positively to urban development?
Secondly, what machinery would allow the national interest, as defined by parliament, to affect a decision made at the local level and with implications for the whole country?
I would have some suggestions to offer in answer to this question of the Prime Minister. He added:
Thirdly and finally: does the enormous increase in the political and financial responsibilities of the municipalities give rise to a need for new constitutional provisions?
The Prime Minister added:
X do not believe that there exists any agency more directly concerned with these questions than this Federation of Mayors and Municipalities.
Who is the official spokesman (those are my own words) of all municipalities across Canada?
Bom from a pressing need to settle the problems that resulted in the cities from the financial crisis of the thirties, your Federation has constantly reviewed the part the municipalities should play, and their relationship with the provincial and federal governments.

[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, I am in the very thick of things. I might say that I have been familiar with the municipal problems for the last twenty years or so. I was on the executive of the Conference of the mayors of central Quebec, which comprises 85 municipalities. I have also been on the executive of the Union of the municipalities of the province of Quebec. I was on the executive of the Canadian Federation of mayors, of which, at one time, I have been the chairman. I took part in conferences of municipalities in the ten provinces of Canada. I attended seminars of municipal associations in the United States and Europe, and each time I set foot on Canadian soil I have noticed an almost incredible thing:	when problems coming
under these three levels of government are dealt with, the spokesmen of the municipal governments are practically ignored. They are treated like backward children and they find themselves constantly at grips with those difficulties that we are discussing, but they are devoid of the means of solving them.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is high time that the country be informed of such a situation. What are the needs of the municipalities? The answer should be at hand, as the municipalities submit these needs every year to the federal government which, unfortunately, be it Liberal or Conservative finds itself immediately in conflict with the provincial governments. These governments cry: "Hands off! The municipalities belong to us."
I believe this to be true. I admit that legally, municipalities are creatures of the provinces, but I also think that that gives the municipalities the right to take part in discussions and, when the time comes to share the revenue, the right to express their opinions. In fact, they are the ones closer to the people and in a better position to suggest solutions, since they have first hand knowledge of the problems facing them each day. And I do not know of any constitutionnal or legal provision which forbids the mayors of Canada to meet wherever they choose to compare notes to try to benefit from the experience of others, to consult those who are more experienced and together to devise solutions which will enable them to carry out their mandate.
Among all those problems facing us, here is how should be handled those coming under the jurisdiction of the three levels of government. Here is an excerpt from a brief entitled Submission to the Government of Canada, submitted by the Canadian Federation of
June 12, 1969

Mayors and Municipalities at the end of April of this year, and I quote:

Who is responsible . . . for housing, for pollution control, for unemployment and for creating new jobs, for devising policies which will bring about a reduction in the cost of money, for keeping prices stable, for assuring the welfare needs of less fortunate Canadians? The locus of responsibility lies somewhere in a limbo of constitutional debate, infringement and obscurity. In seeking the responsibility for any one or more of these, insofar as it will mean access to new tax sources or revenues, the blanket-so to speak-is pulled back and forth between governments; there is considerably less blanket tugging, however, when it comes to enunciating effective policies. Here, the "buck" is passed and, all too frequently, the municipalities-within which such problems actually arise-are left to hold the bag.

Not only are municipalities refused the revenue sources they need, but they are handicapped on the debenture market. They have trouble selling their bonds. I understand there is at present in Canada $60 millions worth of municipal bonds on the shelves, and when they are finally sold, the rates are almost prohibitive, so that the municipality is still at a disadvantage.
I repeat that the provincial governments should once and for all understand that with the urgency and the proliferation of problems only dialogue at the three levels of government will make it possible to find acceptable solutions. For political or other reasons, attempts are being made to prevent that dialogue: In my opinion, it is a perpetuation of discrimination which is at the root of almost all the problems which we are discussing here, and which we find very difficult to solve.
Here are a few of the problems which were discussed by the mayors from all over Canada during their convention in Ottawa. Low cost housing with all the problems involved. Municipalities would be prepared to take action but they cannot afford it.
Mr. Speaker, a few years ago, some pieces of legislation were designed to assist directly the municipalities in providing for the construction of an adequate number of homes.
There was "The municipal... tEnglish]
The municipal winter works incentive program, introduced in 1958, was terminated in 1968. The municipal development and loan fund, established in 1963 (and which should have preferably been a permanent program under which capital funds would have been provided to the provinces to

The Budget-Mr. Mongrain enable them to set up "municipal credit institutions"), was terminated in 1966. A program of federal financial assistance towards urban renewal, first established in 1956 and then given real substance in 1964, has been suspended since late 1968 and now appears to be in serious jeopardy.

-at least restricted to a certain extent. [English]
The federal program of loans and forgiveness of loans for the installation of trunk sewers and the construction of sewage treatment plants, introduced in 1960, appears to be headed for termination. This is a sorry picture-

-say the mayors of Canada.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that the spokesmen of the mayors of Canada are not getting the deal they deserve, considering the serious and extensive problems they have to solve.
There is another problem which is a matter of concern for them: pollution-a serious problem as we all know. I would like to quote here the statement made by a doctor and published in the June 11 issue of La Presse. He had this to say last week, at Pointe-au-Pic:
Water pollution is catching up with us at an alarming rate. I would even go as far as to say that it is definitely out of control. Such was the statement made yesterday by Dr. Richard Nelson, from Hull, who is a member of the Quebec Water Development Committee, and a member of the Quebec Wildlife Federation.
Mr. Speaker, I was reading recently in a research paper that, last year, a special UNESCO committee made up of representatives of various branches of science coming from 55 countries met in Paris where they concluded unanimously that things being as they are, unless drastic steps are taken in just about every country of the world, by the year 2,000, it will be impossible for man and animals to survive on earth. That means that municipalities must soon take steps to deal with water and air pollution. But provincial and federal governments, in some cases, for all sorts of constitutional and other reasons, are not providing those municipalities the means to solve their problems.
There is also the question of fiscal matters. I know that, for several years now, municipalities have asked that a municipal fund be established, some sort of municipal bank to which the federal and provincial governments would contribute funds to enable municipalities to take advantage of the borrowing power of the federal government, or
June 12, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Mongrain at least from the easy credit of the federal government, in order to borrow at more reasonable interest rates.
This formula has been used in Europe for over 110 or 120 years. The communal funds have, we know, proved very successful. However, we are told that it cannot be done here for all kinds of constitutional reasons.
The mayors are also asking that the railway act be amended so that they will not have to pay such a large share of the building costs of railway crossings.
In addition, they are asking-and I believe this sums up their requests-for the right to participate in the constitutional conferences, especially those that deal with fiscal matters, in order to have the opportunity to put forward their views.
I have personally advocated in the house two or three years ago the creation of an intergovernmental advisory commission. This kind of agency exists in the United States and obtains excellent results. Such a commission could be useful in this country. It exists now in a somewhat different form in Canada but the representatives of the municipal administration are not entitled to give their opinion and are not invited to participate in the study or in the research of new means to solve the problems that exist on the three levels of government.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, it is the voice of the Canadian municipalities which I would like to project, and I would like it to be heard far and wide, .so that whose whom I regard as most responsible for this disagreement or for this lack of dialogue between the three levels of government, the provincial administrators, the provincial premiers, the people in charge of municipal affairs, understand that even if we accept the fact that the municipality is, legally speaking, a creature of the province, therefore answerable to the province, its spokemen should nevertheless be treated like adults who are conscious of their responsibilities and who know how to solve the problems of their [DOT]constituents. Therefore, they are entitled to give their opinion on the same basis as other levels of government, because they are not less important than the two others since they are closer to the grass roots and know more than any member or any other government what are the real needs of the people.
What are, for instance, the ways of dealing with the problems of leisure, with the sew-.age, water supply and street problems

created by housing projects, with new parks development, with the fight against pollution and unemployment? How can we overcome the urban transport and development difficulties, in short those things that require capital investment, so as to enable all Canadians to benefit from that reasonable modicum of creature comforts without which, according to St. Thomas Aquinas, no Christian can find salvation.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take advantage of the latitude traditionally permitted in this debate to discuss a matter of urgent importance to the future of Canada. I refer to the disastrous proposal apparently put forward by the government at the closed door sessions of the federal-provincial constitutional conference.
I say "apparently" because it is impossible to be sure whether newspaper stories that
June 12, 1969

emanate from secret conferences are correct in substance or in detail. However, the Globe and Mail, an excellent newspaper in my judgment, has come out with a clearcut statement of a federal plan to allow any two of the four federal senatorial districts, the maritimes, Quebec, Ontario and the west, to veto the use by the Canadian government of the federal spending power through some machinery of a reformed Senate appointed in whole or in part by the provinces.
If this story is true, and I hope it is not, we in our party must hasten to express our view that it is an outrageous proposal, undermining the federal system and ignoring parliamentary control. Such a proposal would constitute a betrayal of the federal government's responsibility to maintain national standards in certain services essential to all Canadians. It would enhance regional disparities, and the whole system of social security as it has grown up would be undermined.
Within such a constitutional strait-jacket we might never have had old age pensions or the Canada Pension Plan. Although I appreciate that now old age pensions are specifically a federal responsibility, the original old age pension plan would no doubt have been vetoed and, at best, postponed. Federal contributions to the hospitalization plan for all Canada would never have come into effect. Without a doubt, the two central regions of Canada would have torpedoed for all of Canada the universal medical plan as recommended by the Hall commission. The Canada Assistance Plan, of which the predecessor of this government was rightly proud, might have been sabotaged.
A more serious aspect of these proposals is that once again they have shown that the government is unwilling to take parliament into its confidence. Here we have sprung, at a federal provincial conference, sweeping proposals which go to the very root of the constitutional structure and functions of parliament. Yet the elected members of parliament, and I believe this includes government supporters as well as members of the opposition, have been given no glimmering, no inkling, of what the proposals contain.
The government of Canada may well be committing itself to the provinces on constitutional amendments which undermine the federal power of dealing effectively with regional disparities. Once the government is formally committed it cannot back down and its supporters cannot defeat or change its proposals without voting lack of confidence in the government. We all know that in practice,
The Budget-Mr. Brewin if the government commits itself in advance, its proposals will be swept through by a majority vote. A commitment by the government without prior consultation with or approval by parliament has the effect of bypassing parliament.
Three of four years ago, and consistently since that date, we in this party and I personally have proposed, as have other members, machinery whereby the need for constitutional change in Canada could be examined by the elected representatives of the Canadian people so that when proposals were made to the provinces they would carry not only the approval of the government of the day but the consensus of parliament itself.
The proposal was for an all-party special committee on the constitution. The former Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, said he approved of this plan, but he did nothing about it. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has never concealed his lack of interest in consulting the representatives of the people on constitutional issues. However, just the other day he announced in the house that at the next session such a committee might be set up. This would be locking the barn door after the horse had been stolen. Can anyone doubt if cut and dried proposals for constitutional change are presented by the government to such a committee the tendency of the committee would be to divide on partisan lines with, on one side, the majority dedicated to endorsing the proposal and, on the other, a minority in all probability dedicated to opposing it?
I want to go back now to the substance of the proposal. It is to give the provinces or groups of representatives in a reformed Senate the power to veto the federal government's use of its constitutional power to tax and spend on certain projects not clearly assigned by the constitution to either jurisdiction. I am well aware that there are two schools of thought in respect of federal use of the spending power. In the province of Quebec, for obvious historical and cultural reasons which one can and does respect, the exercise of the spending power of the government has often been regarded as an unwarranted, if not illegal, invasion of provincial fields of jurisdiction and provincial rights. But in the other provinces, particularly the have-not provinces, the exercise of the federal spending power in shared-cost programs has been absolutely essential and remains so if the people in those provinces are to enjoy any measure of equality in the services to which Canadians as a whole aspire.

June 12, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Brewin We in this party are ready to recognize the strong and natural feelings of the people of Quebec and to concede some means of opting out of these cost-sharing programs without penalty, as a general rule. But to give a veto power to any two out of four regions in Canada and, above all, to senatorial minorities however appointed, would be to hamstring the initiative of the federal government and to deny to other Canadians the security and the standards to which they are entitled. It would be to deny the power of leadership in those fields to the parliament and government of Canada. The potential impact of parliament on the welfare of Canadians would be reduced to virtually nil, and interest in the federal government would consequently diminish if not disappear.
Let it be clear that we in this party do believe that shared-cost programs should generally be administered on a provincial and local basis. We do believe in the continuous and active co-operation of the federal and provincial governments. We do believe that the provision of adequate provincial revenues to carry out the tasks unquestionably within provincial jurisdiction is urgent. What we do not believe in is the abdication of the federal parliament from concern, in co-operation with the provinces, in such fields as housing, social welfare and medicare, and to give an external veto outside parliament is indeed a form of abdication.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
There are in these proposals extremely important implications in the field of taxation. What we are now seeing, I suspect, is a total abandonment of the efforts symbolized by the Rowell-Sirois report to bring order out of chaos in the field of federal-provincial relations. This report was based on three essential principles: first, the removal of competition among the various levels of government in various tax fields through reallocation of responsibilities and the establishment of exclusive areas of taxing jurisdiction; second, the establishment of national standards; third, a system of equalization payments based on fiscal need in relation to national standards rather than on fiscal capacity.
It seems clear from the proposals set out in the Globe and Mail, and from the government's proposal, that the government is proposing to abandon at least the second of these pillars, namely, a strong, rational federal system essential in the long run to Canadian unity. This is the second recent incident which has demonstrated that the people of

Canada elected the present government on the basis of a misunderstanding. The Prime Minister won acclaim all over Canada because he purported to stand for a strong federal government in a strong Canada. We are now seeing that this stance was misleading. The resignation of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), because he discovered this misunderstanding, was the first disillusionment. It became clear to the Prime Minister's former deskmate and second in command that the Prime Minister in fact did not wish a federal structure strong enough to take an effective part in dealing with the housing problems of Canadians.
Now, from behind the closed doors of the federal-provincial conference in the railway station, emerges a plan to emasculate the federal government's spending powers and its ability to deal with regional disparities in social welfare. The man who won election on a "one Canada" slogan bids fair, if the present proposal comes into effect, to become the creator of a "four Canada" monstrosity.
I believe that the effective custodian of the rights of parliament and a federal structure which would preserve a strong central government is parliament itself. I urge my colleagues of all parties to make it clear to the government that it must not proceed to any invasion or erosion of federal constitutional powers without full reference to parliament, without adequate debate in parliament and without final decision by parliament.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

We find in the government's proposal something particularly odious-the notion of conferring a veto power over the action of parliament by some minority representation from a non-elective body, the Senate or the other place, if anybody prefers to call it that. Within a federal system such as we have in Canada there are more than enough roadblocks to effective legislative action to meet the needs of Canadians. It is hardly necessary for the government to create constitutional hazards, which will be the case under this proposal.
Constitutions seem to some people dull and lifeless legal documents, but I remind the house that the welfare of Canadians for whom we are responsible depends in a federal system upon the constitutional framework within which we operate. We in this parliament have a responsibility to the people who elected us to make sure that the constitutional framework, the strong federal Canada in
June 12, 1969

which we believe, is not eroded by any behind-doors conferences that may take place in Ottawa.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address myself this afternoon to two aspects of the budget, the deferred capital cost allowance which has already received a great deal of airing, and the user charges which were justified by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in his budget address. In his speech the minister announced the intention to impose a user charge on persons using commercial air carriers in Canada. I think that is fair and I have no quarrel with this innovation. In making the announcement the minister stated that it is a general policy "to ask those who benefit directly from services or facilities provided by the government to pay charges more in line with the direct cost involved". The minister further stated:
In some cases these charges have not been recently revised to reflect current levels of costs or values of services and we are carrying out a systematic review and revision of these charges. We shall probably introduce some new charges as well.
I do not have any reason to argue with these statements in so far as they represent a general policy. I think it is a wise policy. It stands up well under scrutiny when it is applied in the manner which the minister specifically indicated in his budget speech. But I would like to caution the minister that this policy must be scrutinized in each particular case to which it is thought it might logically be applied.
There may well be instances when to insist upon adherence to the general policy would be unjust, impractical or unsupportable on any other ground. My experience leads me to mention precisely one such case. I refer to the charges levied on the use of certain Crown property located within the national parks of Canada. More particularly, I am concerned with Waterton Lakes National Park, Banff National Park and Jasper National Park, all of which are within my riding. These are the outstanding examples of Canada's national parks system-indeed, of parks systems anywhere in the world.
I know that a number of hon. members were fortunate to visit both Banff and Jasper last week, and perhaps they learned about some of the matters which are causing the people of these parks a great deal of concern. While I know that many hon. members have visited one or more of the mountain parks in Alberta, many others have not yet had the
The Budget-Mr. Sulatycky opportunity to do so. Those who have paid a visit almost surely did so as part of a vacation and therefore may not have become acquainted with the economic and administrative aspects of the parks operation. For this reason I think it is important that I devote some time to consideration of the operation of these parks and how they are affected by the declared policy that those who benefit shall pay the cost.
Jasper, Waterton Lakes, Banff, and Lake Louise which is within Banff National Park, are known throughout the world. Of the several million visitors who enter one or more of these areas each year, a high percentage come from outside our borders. To many people any one of these names may better describe Canada than Toronto, Montreal or any other place name in this country. To them Banff, Jasper, Lake Louise or Waterton may epitomize Canada as a country of spectacular vistas, richly endowed by nature, peaceful, serene and occupied by an industrious, courteous people.
In order to serve these visitors, Canadian tourists especially, when they visit these areas the government has for many years actively promoted the establishment of tourist facilities such as hotels, motels, restaurants, service stations and other businesses of the type which cater and appeal to the travelling public. At the same time, one transcontinental railway traverses the Rocky Mountains at the exact location of Banff National Park, and the other crosses the same mountains by cutting through Jasper National Park. More recently the trans-Canada highway was constructed through Banff, and now an equally important and highly utilized road, the Yellowhead highway, bisects Jasper National Park. In addition, certain other national communication and transportation channels have, because of geography and physiography, been compelled to pass through these parks.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The net result is that the demand for tourist services at certain key points, coupled with active promotion for many years by the government of adequate facilities, further coupled with the needs of transcontinental transportation and communication, has resulted in the development at certain locations within these national parks of communities filling these established needs and demands. The result is that at both the Banff and Jasper townsites we now have communities of more than 3,000 persons each, and at Water-ton and Lake Louise communities of much
10062	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Sulatycky smaller dimensions but in all cases very much like any other town or village in Canada except tor the tact that these park communities occupy awe-inspiring geographic locations. The geographic location would be the only factor distinguishing one of the park communities from any non-park community in the mind of the casual visitor. But in actuality they are very different.
All land within the national parks is owned by the Crown. There is no privately held land. This is the basic difference between the communities within and outside the national parks. It is1 within this system of land holding in the parks that the application of the general policy stated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) breaks down. I will not at this time dispute the basic concept of this system since an essential element of it, the lease renewable in perpetuity, is now before the Supreme Court of Canada and also because that part of the problem is not wholly within any aspect of the budget as presented by the Minister of Finance. But the matter of compensation expected by the Crown from those persons who occupy Crown-owned land under a lease is one which is certainly described by the minister in his previously quoted remarks, and it is also one which deserves the full and careful consideration of this house in the context of those remarks.
I want to examine the situation which exists at the present time in the national parks of Banff, Jasper and Waterton. The federal government decided many years1 ago that in each of these cases there was an area which should be preserved as a park for future generations of Canadians. It needed these areas as national parks and it promoted them as such. Large amounts of money were expended in the interest of all Canadians for the development of these parks. In order to get people to establish necessary services within the area set aside as. a park the Crown granted leases which contained a clause providing that such leases will be renewed time after time, in perpetuity. People moved in and accepted these leases. The government charged a small land rental, a nominal sum, for the use of this land. These leaseholders built improvements on the land and when, in the ordinary course of events, the leaseholders or their successors were required to dispose of the property, new inhabitants of the park purchased the improvements and the unused term of the lease. The balance of the lease term is valuable because it carries the right of renewal. In many cases a very respectable sum is paid for the unused term of a lease for this reason.

DEBATES	June 12, 1969
Once a leaseholder, an individual must assume certain obligations. He must pay the land rental to the Crown. In addition, he must pay the ordinary school and hospital taxes levied under provincial legislation. Furthermore, since the land rental does not cover any services, the government compels him to pay a water and sewerage rate to cover the cost of providing such services. In the meantime the Crown continues to expend funds on the development of the park.
It is noted by Crown officials that the revenues realized from the national parks do not equal the amounts expended on them. At the same time, other officials say that the residents of the parks should not enjoy any economic advantage over residents outside the parks, nor should they be at any economic disadvantage. The implication is that in so far as the cost of holding and maintaining property within the parks is concerned, it should not be a great deal more nor a great deal less than the cost of holding similar property in a community outside a federal park. This is logical.
However, it costs the federal government a substantial sum each year to operate and maintain the townsites. They are maintained at a standard well above those of any similar non-park community, not for the benefit of the people who live there but in the interests of the country as a whole. The intent is to benefit those people who find enjoyment in visiting the natural splendour found within the parks. It is only incidental that some of the benefits accrue to the people who are required to live in the parks.
Much of the cost of the operation of the townsites is directly attributable to the services provided in order that the townsites can cope with the demands of large numbers of tourists. The influx of tourists in the summer has the effect of multiplying five to tenfold the population which relies on the services of the government. I submit that under these circumstances it is inequitable to expect the permanent residents of the townsites to pay a rental more closely related to the costs of the services provided. To do so would depart from the proposition that these residents suffer no economic disadvantage nor receive any advantage.
The whole scope of the administration of townsites within the national parks has been a matter of concern for some years now. Many problems are involved in addition to the ones I have been discussing. Almost ten years ago the Institute of Local Government
June 12, 1969

at Queens University conducted a study for the department of northern affairs and national resources, then responsible for national parks. This study inquired into various aspects of townsite administration. The report which resulted from the study is commonly called the Crawford report. It is enlightening to read some of the passages of this report in the light of recent actions- by the national parks branch and in the light of the policy which expects the recipient of services to bear the cost more directly.
Before I read from this report I should point out that there is1 no municipal government in the park townsites. Elsewhere in Canada a citizen has. the right of representation in municipal, provincial and federal government, but not in a park townsite. The position has been that so long as the federal government pays the cost of the townsite there should be no right to municipal selfgovernment in the townsites. So long as the federal government bore a large share of the costs the inhabitants of these townsites, quite rightly, did not expect a decisive say in their operation. The Crawford report had this to say on the subject:
Local self-government involves a willingness on the part of the inhabitants to assume the responsibilities and obligations of government and a willingness to meet a significant portion of the cost. Without this willingness, local self-government will not function satisfactorily. Without the obligation to meet a significant part of the cost, there can be no real sense of responsibility in public spending.
If this is- a compelling argument against self-government in the park townsites, and I think it is, then as soon as the obligation to meet a significant part of the cost is transferred to the inhabitants the same reasoning becomes equally compelling in favour of selfgovernment. I merely want to mention this aspect of the problem now because I intend to deal with it in much greater detail in the coming months.
The Crawford report underscored other aspects of the park townsites operation. It found that the rents being paid to the government were in general very low and also that some lessees were much more favourably treated than others. At the same time it also pointed out that, in addition to rent being paid to the Crown, lessees were paying school taxes and charges for water and sewer services as well as hospital taxes. At the rates prevailing today the average home owner in any one of the townsites is paying, in various rates and levies, an amount equal to approximately 75 per cent of the taxes he would be
The Budget-Mr. Sulatycky required to pay on similar property situated outside the parks. All park residents would be extremely willing to pay an increased rental to bring this percentage to 100. This would involve an increase of 33J per cent. No one would object. But it appears that the general policy as stated in the budget speech will be applied, and in the year 1970 residents of national park townsites will be expected to bear increases ranging from 100 per cent to 1,400 per cent, I suggest that this is unjust. The application of the general policy breaks down in this instance.
There is one more aspect of the matter of charging increased land rentals which I feel cannot go unmentioned. I refer to the inequities in the manner in which the rental increases will affect different pieces of land. Up to 1949 land was, generally speaking, available without tender or upset price. In other words, land was available for the taking. In that year the practice was changed to provide for the lessor to pay for land which he was leasing. In effect, he was buying a lease. In the words of the Crawford report:
The tenderer then offered what price he was prepared to pay for a particular lot knowing when he did so what annual rental he would have to pay in addition to the price of the lot.
This meant, of course, that a bidder would be prepared to pay a higher price for a lot if he knew that it carried a low yearly rental. In 1952 the procedure was changed again, but the price of a lot was still inversely proportionate to the annual land rental. A departmental memo of that year stated:
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
In establishing the prevailing upset prices for lots in park townsites, the department has taken into consideration the comparatively low lot rentals payable for lots used for residential purposes, as well as the fact that park residents, whether permanent or transient, pay no general tax rate and make no contribution towards normal townsite maintenance.
Obviously, it was the intention to nullify the lack of taxes by a higher upset price.
The effect of the department charging a substantial price for a lot is readily perceivable: it immediately established a lot value, whether that lot was purchased from the crown or from a previous leaseholder. The result was that any lot leased or lease purchased was in fact paid for by the purchaser. This situation obtained until recently when the procedure was again changed and leases on lots are now no longer sold by the Crown. Rather a lease is granted and the lessee
10064	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Sulatycky understands that he will be required to pay a substantial land rental. Then, on the basis of the existing procedure the department establishes increased land rentals and attempts to justify the same by claiming that the leaseholder possesses an advantage in that he does not have to pay for his lot. While that may be true in some cases, in the vast majority he did. And it does not make any difference that the price paid may have been to a previous leaseholder rather than to the crown. It was crown policy which encouraged the price structure of leasehold sales.
These are some of the problems connected with townsites in parks. There are many more, but these are the ones which stem directly from the policy respecting user charges stated in the budget speech. I hope the minister and his colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), will take cognizance of the weakness of the policy in certain situations and make the necessary adjustments to ensure fair treatment of those citizens who reside in townsites in national parks.
I want to speak briefly on the matter of the deferral of capital cost allowances on commercial projects in any city of more than
50,000	people in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. A number of members, particularly those in the opposition, have been critical of this action. Even greater cries of anguish have been heard from some municipal officials. They, of course, are given to self-concern only and have no need to think of the nation generally. For my part, even if the minister had risen in his place and announced in as few words as possible this deferral action, his budget speech would have been highly commendable.
I recognize that the primary purpose of this step is to hold down the fires of inflation which are reaching inferno-like proportions. However, it is the secondary effect of this measure, that of contributing to the easing of regional disparities, which most appeals to me.
By regional disparities, I do not mean only the disparities which exist as between, say, southern Ontario and western Newfoundland, for example. Indeed, I harbour no illusion that the minister's plan will in any way transfer some benefit from Toronto to anywhere in the Atlantic provinces. I am referring generally to the disparities of economic opportunity which exists within Canada. It will readily be acknowledged that the greatest opportunities for economic advancement exist within the confines of more or less a

DEBATES	June 12, 1969
score of the largest cities in this country. A few miles outside these confines, the opportunities are drastically reduced.
But while there is this disparity, there is also competition between these large cities and the smaller communities in the hinterland. The basic competition is for capital. Many of the smaller communities show a substantial rate of growth, but they do not grow at the same rate as the large cities. They must compete with the cities for capital, and what they receive is not at all proportionate to what they and the larger cities require. In the end, the disparity is increased.
This provision in the budget will certainly not help any municipality which is far removed from any of the 22 cities affected, nor will it help any area which is in a state of recession; but it certainly should prove to be an asset in the search for capital by many smaller expanding communities. I hope it will have this effect. If it has, I know of many areas which will benefit. I can think of a number of expanding towns in my own area, towns such as Blairmore, Coleman, Turner Valley, Black Diamond, Canmore, Hinton, Ed-son, Drayton Valley, Whitecourt, Fox Creed and Grande Cache.
If the measure does not have the desired effect, as members opposite have been quick to predict, may I suggest that rather than having gone too far in this matter of deferral of depreciation the Minister of Finance will not have gone far enough. Perhaps serious consideration should be given to the repeal of all provisions for capital cost allowances on all buildings throughout Canada. We all know that the people who benefit the most are those who least need this kind of benefit. In its place, and as a measure to assist in the development of Canada, new provision should be made for capital cost allowances in those areas of Canada which are economically strong but do not have the capital drawing powers of the more highly urbanized cities in Canada.
I am pleased to be able to congratulate the Minister of Finance on this budget and particularly on the fact that it is a balanced one.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity of saying what I think of the present economic situation, of the supposedly balanced budget-a thing that we had not seen in a long time-which was presented to the people.
June 12, 1969	COMMONS
Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss this matter, namely whether it is important and justifiable to balance a budget. The question is to how are we going to do it, and whether it will help Canadians or be a nuisance to them.
Will not the fact of balancing the budget at this moment be harmful for the Canadian economy? I say, here and now, that the Canadian economy will be adversely affected, because to balance the national budget, it will be necessary to unbalance the taxpayer's budget.
This is, Mr. Speaker, where we stand with a balanced budget under the present system.
The Conservatives have tried to balance the budget when they were in power. The Liberals have been doing the same for many years because they have been in power for quite a long time. The Conservatives have not been in power very long, all in all, during the past 20 years. The Liberals have been at the helm almost continuously for some 30 years now. The Progressive Conservatives were only transients, but neither party has ever succeeded in balancing the tax payer's budget.
It is important to balance the budget, provided that does not throw the taxpayers' budget out of balance. Taxpayers are responsible for that budget. They pay for that. Depriving the taxpayer of his purchasing power to balance a budget, to please and serve big finance, is contrary to good sense.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
It is preferable in the present system that budgets be unbalanced. It is awful to balance a budget, thereby throwing the whole Canadian economy out of balance, and keeping in misery, in poverty, in insecurity, a large part, and I could safely say, 80 per cent of the population. People are plunged in anarchy for the sake of a balanced budget.
They speak of inflation and they want to solve the problem inherent to it. As soon as the population is threatened with a certain economic unbalance, we are told that we are in a period of inflation. The people do not have the right to balance their family budget, they never have the right to do so; but the financier has the right to balance his own. He has the right to organize the inflationary economic systems. Under this system, the people are threatened with inflation and deflation and they go from one recession to another. In times of inflation, the watchword from the financiers is: austerity for the people. That means we must tighten our belts then.
The Budget-Mr. Latulippe
In times of deflation, the financiers impose tight money policies, allow the increase in interest rates, which brings about ruin, bankruptcy, unemployment and misery. That is strangling, tightening the belt to the last notch.
This is1 what the so-called balanced budget is doing. To be realist, the financial system should conform to realities of production and needs. Now those realities are disregarded. No consideration is given to the real facts or to the physical facts. The purpose in balancing the budget is to give bigger interests to high finance, to bleed the people white and to put them at the mercy of high finance that exploits them in a criminal way.
To act in this way is criminal. Money should go where the needs are and the needs are felt by the people. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) set forth, a short while ago, the needs of the people, of the municipalities and of the provinces. He stated that money was required to meet such needs but he did not ask the government where it was to be found. He did not ask the government to initiate reforms to change our vicious financial system that deprives the population of its freedom and its right to live decently. That he did not say and will not say, because that might not serve the purpose of some supporters or some financiers, in the government itself or in the country at large.
We have never experienced a viable economic balance in Canada for decades. We have never balanced our budget as concerns corporations or individuals. The prices of services have been raised as never before in Canadian history.
Indeed, it is easy to balance the budget, if all the services provided to the provinces and municipalities to promote our economy are curtailed. Investments have been cut but the interest rate was allowed to rise, which is the main cause of inflation and will lead the great majority of the people to deflation.
Inflation is due to 20 per cent of the population, while 80 per cent suffer from deflation. Who cares? Yet the budget must be balanced.
Mr. Speaker, since I came here in 1962, both Tories and Liberals have attempted to balance the budget. The Liberal or Conservative opposition raised a strong protest and said that unemployment was worse than ever and that the government should do something to deal with unemployment and poverty, to foster the development of municipalities and school boards and promote housing. In fact, no houses had been built in ten years and
June 12, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Latulippe nothing had been done to balance the budget during the same period. The whole economy was lagging behind, and was practically at a standstill.
The Conservatives, under the present system, tried to put the economy back on its feet. They devised some measures to promote winter works, to help municipalities and provinces and to alleviate unemployment and poverty, which were rampant in this country.
But to that end, it was necessary to accept an unbalanced budget, to raise loans, to pay interest rates in order to finance provincial, municipal and school debts. For that purpose, the debt was increased, and the federal budget was alarmingly out of balance.
Then the Liberals came to power. The people were unhappy because the debt had been increased, the economic problem remained unsolved, for there were still pockets of dire poverty in the country. Adequate solutions and possible improvements had been merely touched on and a few improvements had been made.
The Liberals contend: the Conservatives have spent too much, they have increased the debt of the country. We will have to increase taxes, to cancel joint programs, make a cut here and a cut there. That is what has been done in the last few years, and it is claimed that eventually it will be possible to balance the budget of the financial interests, but not that of the government. We will allow finance to collect interests of 10, 12, 15, 24 per cent, to sweat the people, to lay down the law and, at the same time, we will bring the Canadian economy down to its lowest level.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The Progressive Conservatives will tell the people: "The Liberals gave you nothing and did nothing for you." Then they will try to get back into office with exactly the same administration, the same wagon, the same old run-down jalopy which is done with, but instead of changing the old crate they change the driver. This has been going on for decades now.
And so for Canadians at large, things remain static or grow worse, because every time something is being done for the people, we get into new debts which we are unable to repay. And when a group such as ours, demands a balanced economy, a reform of our financial system the financing of our provinces and municipalities with the same appropriations available to us now, but interest free, they say we are crackpots,

whacky, simpletons, mentally deficient and off our rocker. But I wonder who is mostly off his rocker at the present time and if one of the two parties have really found a solution. I have heard several Conservatives or Liberal members speak on the budget. But not a single one suggested even a shadow of a solution to the problem. However, they want to take over, and to govern. They blame our present leaders without offering however any concrete solution for balancing our economy.
It is not this budget which is going to set our topsy-turvy economic situation right again. First, in order to balance the budget, there should be a reduction in expenditures and capital investments. For instance, the winter works programs have been cancelled and a number of measures liable to increase the purchasing power, which would enable the human being to fulfill itself, the various bodies to build, to expand, to give the nation that to which it is entitled.
But all this progress is being delayed to allow the financiers to exploit the people, to extract frightful interest rates and neither the government nor any government member has any say in the matter except the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres who said a while ago that the interest rates are exorbitant and that something should be done to remedy the situation. He is the only Liberal member I have heard take the people's side rather than that of the financiers.
We have known wars and crises and we are still living in a period of inflation and deflation because we never had a balanced system.
Let us take, for example, the war which the United States are waging against Viet Nam. You will tell me that the war is not ended though it is about to end. However, for the five years which this war has been going on, we have seen unparalleled prosperity in the United States. They spoke neither of deflation nor of inflation because everything was going well. Now, they talk of peace. Although it is yet to come, the problem of inflation is already being raised. By means of taxes, levies and exorbitant interest rates, they want to take away from the people the money Canadians earned during the war, in order to put it in the hands of the high finance,, which will exploit the people again by imposing a 10 per cent rate of interest.
Mr. Speaker, that is what we have come to on account of a topsy-turvy international economic system. As soon as the United States get themselves in this kind of a mess, Canada
June 12, 1969	COMMONS
suffers; she immediately raises her rates of interest. The Bank of Canada immediately increases its discount rate instead of lowering it, in order to lend money to the Americans.
Mr. Speaker, instead of cashing in on credit with an American guarantee, we prefer raising our rates of interest to the level established by the Americans, to prevent them from coming here, and buying our products. As for the high finance system, not a single one among you condemns it. Not a single one among you realizes what is going on. We are told it is a normal thing to balance a budget. We are told this is sound administration, and adequate and rational way of doing things, while the opposite is true. It is the most illogical administraton we have ever seen and we shall ever see in any country.
What does the present budget amount to? I say with certainty that the increase in the debt service means that the Canadian people will pay the highest interest in their whole history, and statistics bear me out on that point.
Let us1 just think of the Post Office department. Postal tariffs became perhaps 500 times higher than they should have been perhaps even they were set a thousand per cent too high. Indeed, they have been increased tremendously in order to balance the budget. We blame the minister, Mr. Speaker, because he is primarily responsible but he is not the only one. All hon. members are to be blamed, all those who accept such a situation.
Looking at the interest of the debt, we see that it amounted to $817 million in 1961, to $1,147 million in 1964-65, and to $2,102 million in 1968-69. There will be a fairly large increase in 1969-70 since bonds will be redeemed at the new current interest rate.
The minister wants to check inflation by increasing the interest of the debt and keeping taxes as they are. He is strangling the taxpayers. The budget is to be balanced at the expense of the taxpayers, that is by upsetting even further the individuals' budget, to balance that of big finance, by keeping higher interest rates which will give more money to-

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in making some remarks in connection with the proposal made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), usually termed the budget speech, I first want to tell the house how impressed I was with the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). He referred to the delegation of responsibility by those who have been entrusted with responsibility by the people of a country. I have always had a very strong opinion relative to the delegation of responsibility.
Generally speaking, people are elected by their friends and neighbours who know them
10068	COMMONS DEBATES	June 12, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Flemming well. They are elected because of the knowledge which others have of them and because of the things they promise to carry out. They are elected because they have a certain policy and have indicated they will carry out that policy. I am anxious to express my disapproval in no uncertain terms of any suggestion that there be some delegation of control of federal spending to any other body in Canada, thus removing control from a strong central government. This was the suggestion to which the hon. member for Greenwood referred this afternoon.
We have before us a motion by the Minister of Finance, and since it is very short I will quote it:
That this house approves in general the budgetary policy of the government.
I think we have to consider the question of whether or not the government has changed its policy. We have to decide whether it is the same policy that has been in effect since 1965, and even since 1963. I cannot think of anyone in a better position to express approval or otherwise than a man who has been a member of the government and who, within the last three or four weeks, found reasons to resign from it.
I have here in my hand an article from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald headlined, "Hellyer Takes Swipe at Policy." This refers to the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) who should know all about government policy. The article bears a London, Ontario, dateline and reads:
Mr. Hellyer attacked what he called excessive emphasis on constitutional reform and not enough on bread and butter issues.
The reason I quote it is this gentleman should certainly know all about government policy, yet he says it is not the proper policy for the country and, as the headline says, he takes a swipe at it.
A headline in the Globe and Mail of June 11 stated, "Hellyer Wants Government to be More Businesslike." He implies that the government does not have the proper amount of business ability. All who are not prejudiced and whose eyes are not clouded by bias know the government has indicated absolutely no business ability in the way it has handled the affairs of the nation over the last few years. We would not be in the position we are in today if it had shown business ability. So, this is the headline, "Hellyer wants government to be more businesslike". This is the statement of a man who knows all about the government because he was a member of it. Here is

another statement in the Toronto Star having to do with government policy. It reads, "Hellyer says government to blame for financial mess." Those are his words; they are not mine. We are being asked to express approval of the budgetary policy of the government when a former member of that government finds he cannot accept it. He makes speeches and tells the people of Canada the reasons he cannot support it. It seems to me this is a very difficult motion to support. I suppose our friends opposite will say they have to support it because that is their job; but that is not the job of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). It will be interesting to see how he deals with this motion.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
So far as I am concerned, has this motion been qualified to some extent then probably I might believe the government had a change of heart, that it had changed its policy and that the new policy might be acceptable. But this1 motion does not indicate there has been any change, and therefore it seems to me it would be very difficult to accept the motion. Then, we have an amendment by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. (Lambert) to the effect that this house regrets the continuing inability of the government to curb the relentless increase in the cost of living since 1965. How could anyone vote against that amendment? I repeat the words "regrets the continuing inability of the government to curb the relentless increase in the cost of living". That is sometimes known in polite terms as inflation. Then, the amendment goes on to say, "while increasing the hardship on the unemployed, the poor, pensioners, farmers, and other victims of the just society". I think I remember where that phrase "just society" originated, but the way things are going I think the spelling of the word should be changed to j-e-s-t instead of j-u-s-t because that would seem to be more appropriate.
To my hon. friend opposite who interjected may I say there is more joy in heaven for sinners who repent than for all the others; so there is some chance for my hon. friend opposite. The other night we had a vote and the government marshalled all its forces to defeat the subamendment. That was the first time since the budget debate started that the government front benches had been filled. Most of the time they are nearly empty. Tonight, they are nearly empty. I do not think it is entirely because I am speaking; I hope it is not. No members1 of the cabinet are present,
June 12, 1969

but there are some other men present who I hope have some influence. I think they should consider very sincerely whether the committee system is a success it the committee system results in some members losing interest in attending the debates of this house to the extent that would seem to be indicated by the lack ot attendance here tonight.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where are your members?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think our members are attending fairly well, but whether or not they are in their seats, we are not responsible for conducting the affairs of the country. I suggest to hon. members opposite that perhaps they should examine themselves to see whether or not they are making a proper contribution. I think we should give the Minister of Finance some credit because usually he is in his seat, even though he makes his presence known mostly by interruptions.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister is not there now. There are no ministers over there.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can get along without them. As a result of defeating the amendment proposed by the New Democratic party, the members of the government have said in effect that they refuse to consider any measure for the relief of people who are obliged to live on incomes which are below the average. They voted down the amendment. The government has said, in effect, that they will not grant relief in that way. The Minister of Finance, in his speech, has said that he will grant this relief by dealing with inflation and by bringing down prices.
I submit that since the government has indicated its lack of interest in tax reduction, it has decided it must address itself to a reduction in the cost of living. How does the government propose to do this? Well, the other day the minister told us how they propose to do it. I think, however, it would be a good thing if some of our friends opposite would elucidate on how they intend to deal with the matter of inflation. They have not done so. It seems to me the only action they have taken has been the acceptance of the increase in the price of money, the increase in the interest rate. Presumably, this is so that people will not proceed with projects but will postpone them until money is more plentiful and less expensive. With this postponement will come a lessening of employment and people will seek employment elsewhere. In my opinion, there is a more direct way in

The Budget-Mr. Flemming which the government could do this. The government could insist-I say this most advisedly-on a reduction in wasteful projects. This should apply not only to governmental waste but also to waste by Crown corporations which are dependent on this government and parliament for their operating funds.
I think the Minister of Finance should be very firm with the bureaucracy which is increasing numerically. Every single person added becomes a proponent of some type of government expenditure in order to justify his existence. I have had some experience in other places and I suggest that it is common for the importance of a department to be judged by the amount of money it spends. I presume this is still the case. It is time the Minister of Finance did something about this. He will certainly have to do something about it if he expects us to support this motion which indicates that we approve the budgetary policy of the government. He will have to indicate that he intends to do something about it. Does he know, in the case of the Crown corporations, what expenditures have been suggested or even approved? In the first portion of his budget speech he glibly stated that we are now getting a firmer grip upon the national finances and bringing them under more effective control.
When have the national finances been under effective control? I should like some gentleman opposite to tell me when this has happened because there is no indication of it so far as I am concerned. We know the remedy for inflation is not some pleasant medicine. If anyone has this idea he should get rid of it because it is not true. The required improvement can be brought about only by some bitter medicine. The health of the patient, in this case national finances, can be improved only by taking some bitter medicine. The final result will be some improvement in the degree of inflation or even the curing of a portion of it.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I acknowledge freely that the intention of the government to live within its income and not go to the money market to borrow is in itself a constructive step. I give the minister and the government full marks for that, because this leaves the door open for private business to borrow the money it needs.
In this budget speech the Minister of Finance announced that the 3 per cent surtax would be continued until the end of 1970. He said last October it would be terminated in a
June 12, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Flemming year. His reason lor changing his mind and not carrying out this commitment is that this taxation is required for economic stabilization and not for revenue. He uses this word "revenue", but that is just the old word "taxation" dressed up in new clothes. There is no other word for it except "taxation". This tax must come out of the pockets of the people of Canada. Supposing we were to acaept as valid the argument that the Minister of Finance had to levy this tax to stabilize the economy, then this would entail a responsibility on him to see that the tax money thus received was used for the purpose of balancing the budget, of lessening the need for borrowing and for fighting inflation. For this reason, and only for this reason, can this tax money be used for the very worthy purpose of lessening the cost of living.
The reduction, and even an attempt at elimination of waste and extravagance, is one way to combat inflation. The basic principle of a stabilized currency is that we live within our income in good times, thus paving the way for priming the pump by an infusion of borrowed money in hard times. That is as simple as it can be, but this policy has not been carried out by this government. That is why no one, unless he has some other motivation, could possibly vote for this motion before the house tonight.
Investment money pours in because people feel, on the basis of previous performance, that this is a safe country since the people have a sense of responsibility. This is what happens when the world community sees a country balancing its budget. The people invest their money because they feel it is safe and that the government is doing something about the situation. All we have heard or witnessed has been a lot of idle words from different ministers of finance, time and time again.
These ministers of finance said they were conscious of so and so but that they had to do such and such, so on and so on. Finally, we wind up with a fiscal situation as bad as ever. This time we are going to end up with $250 million. Let me tell the Minister of Finance that the Liberal government which enjoyed the type of reputation which was desirable was the Liberal government of Mr. St. Laurent. There is no question about that. The federal government of those days not only lived within its income, it actually reduced the debt during some years and, as a result, the cost of living remained fairly constant. People were able to balance their own budgets and live within their own incomes.

At this time I should like to deal with the matter of tariffs, but because I may not have sufficient time, before I talk about the tariff changes which the minister announced in his first budget. I should refer to another matter. The matter I wish to bring to his attention is something the government has indicated it has in mind. I refer to regional disparity. Let me bring this to the attention of the minister and all those influential members of the Liberal caucus who are within the sound of my voice. I presume they are all influential just as my friend, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai), is influential, along with the rest of them over there if they have any sense at all-sometimes I doubt it.
Surely, the minister already has knowledge of the situation in the maritime provinces, especially New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. The government should devote some attention to this problem which has a reasonable opportunity of affecting this important area. This course is not going to cost the government anything. It should make representations, and I am sure the minister has been approached along these lines, to the United States leading to the elimination of the tariffs on potatoes imposed by our next door neighbour.
Before beginning my remarks on this subject, let me point out to the minister that both New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island have a very close interest in the production of potatoes. Their soil is well suited to this production. I have always felt that so far as our part of the country is concerned, we should place an emphasis on our natural advantages rather than on our disadvantages. One of the biggest advantages in the mari-times over other parts of Canada is that the soil is very good for growing potatoes. This crop is very important to the economy of these two provinces. I know the minister might say that he cannot do anything about free trade with the United States in respect of potatoes because the population of that country is 200 million compared to the 20 million population here.
Let me give you some information about this situation, Mr. Speaker. Since our area comprises a portion of Canada which unfortunately qualifies under the heading of regional disparity, it appears very logical that any action leading to an improvement in the general standard of living in our area should be explored. There is nothing wrong with that. I am now talking about the potato industry in
June 12, 1963

the Atlantic provinces, especially in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
Let me first state the objective which, very simply, is this: Free trade between Canada and the United States in potatoes. Why should this be an objective? Because under the general heading of fruit and vegetables we bring into Canada each year from the United States over $200 million worth of products, and we sell them only 20 per cent of that amount.
