subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, and I thank hon. members of the house for this privilege.
In 1965 we exported $39 million in fruit and vegetables and we imported $200 million worth. In 1966 we exported $34 million in fruit and vegetables and we imported $210 million worth. In 1967 we exported $40 million worth of fruit and vegetables and imported $217 million worth. In commenting on those figures I should like to use the words of Harrison McCain of Florenceville, New Brunswick, the president of McCain Food Ltd., probably the largest food producers in Canada. This industry, to a great extent, exists in my constituency. This company has processing plants in many areas. Mr. McCain uttered these words:
This is a drastic imbalance of trade and on this basis we have a perfect right to ask for duty free entry of our potatoes to help correct this imbalance.
In the same public document Mr. McCain reported that, in respect of potatoes alone, we imported more than we exported, the figure being 9.2 million cwt. imported as against 7.3 million exported. In other words, 20 million people bought more from a country with 200 million than that country bought from us.
This morning at the public accounts committee we were examining the remissions under the auto pact. The thought occurred to me that we might work out an agreement whereby we receive a fair share of the United States market for New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island Potato production by special arrangement. That is what this auto pact was, it was a special arrangement, and the government did not seem to have any difficulty working that out. We have a special arrangement with regard to oil and there does not seem to be any difficulty, or at least no administrative difficulty.
The Budget-Mr. Gibson
New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island produce something less than 10 per cent of the United States market requirements for potatoes. I know the government of New Brunswick has taken this matter up with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and I have no doubt that the Minister of Finance is familiar with it. I believe the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) has been approached in this regard.
Let me add my voice, with all the force and emphasis of which I am capable, to the voices of all those who have approached the government to request negotiations with the United States on the question of duty free potatoes, in both directions, with special attention to the hazardous state of this industry in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. I say to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) that it is just as important to revive and save an industry as it is to go to the expense of creating a new one.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I say this, Mr. Speaker, because a great many people are involved in this problem and the way we handle it.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, several points made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) on Tuesday should not go unchallenged. First, he misinterpreted the Carter report and was in error when he indicated that the budget overlooks tax reform. The Carter report in fact deals with all taxpayers, be they pensioners, widows or wage earners, on the same basis. The impression the hon. member sought to leave was that we should have treated these problems differently and that the Carter report so indicated. Perhaps the hon. member has failed to grasp the significance of the regional technique introduced into the budget for the first time this year. He is probably unaware that this technique was also recommended in the Carter report. We have had a long and interesting debate on the budget. So far, it appears to have been accepted by the country as a whole with enthusiasm as a progressive tax reform budget.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Time will tell.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course, there are always wild-eyed socialists who see no good in any reforms except neo-communistic measures which completely stifle initiative and leave the economy in a strait jacket, as is the case

June 12, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Gibson today under the Labour government of the United Kingdom. It is indeed fortunate that the pessimistic thinking of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) no longer prevails in this country. He had no words of kindness for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson); only bitter sarcasm tinged with bulbous pomp and ceremony. However, gradually the opposition parties will grasp the brilliance of the budget plan and will realize that the regional approach to financial problems in Canada is practical and, of course, is one that will better balance the regional development of this great country.
The hon. member who has just resumed his seat, spoke with eloquence, as he always does, about the unbalanced treatment accorded by the federal government to the problem of inflation. I suggest that his words are a little too premature, when it is quite apparent to all of us in this country that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in calling the federal-provincial conference which is in session at the present time, is urgently grappling with the problem of inflation. The Prime Minister is dealing with a very difficult problem in a humane and practical manner. This is demonstrated by the intensive effort being put forward to make the conference a success.
The Prime Minister and the provincial premiers are not facing the country under the glare of publicity. They are seriously engaged in an effort to change our great constitution. Let us hope they succeed. Why do I think they will succeed? Yesterday a press release was issued by the Prime Minister and the premiers of the provinces which indicated that spending power has been given top priority and that the Prime Minister has explained to the premiers representing the provinces of this great country that we will try and deal with the problem on a federal basis. Therefore, if two of the four regions do not wish to enter a scheme, they do not have to do so. This is a humane approach to dealing with the problem of inflation.
If the Minister of Finance had in his budget spelled out a great many detailed methods of trying to deal with inflation, would he not look stupid if the programs he proposed could not be implemented because the provinces would not co-operate? I suggest it was much sounder for the Minister of Finance to outline the general principles of how he would do this, then iron it out with the provincial premiers and come into the house with a concrete plan. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is a much better approach to the problem.

We on this side of the house agree that fiscal restraint is the foundation for a check upon inflation. In this way we shall succeed in easing strains upon capital markets. The Prices and Incomes Board set up under the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) presents this country with a real challenge in dealing with inflationary pressures. This is a new approach to the problem and we, as Canadians, can counteract the forces which cause inflation. It may be that in concert we can agree not to buy certain goods if the prices of those goods are increased. Perhaps we can find a method of using television and radio in a way that is not dictatorial but expresses the free will of the people in their distaste of enterprises which have selfish interests at heart. If the Prices and Incomes Board can succeed in this area, with the aid of the Canadian consumer, we will have achieved a new method of dealing with our economic evils. In fact, a new force, the force of consumers' associations, may be able to organize against unfair price and wage increases. I welcome the efforts of the government to start work in this direction.
I submit that the Kennedy round tariff reductions will help to increase price competition and resistance to increased costs. The hon. member for Kootenay West asked, what is the government doing about unemployment? I wonder where he has been. The answer is that we have established the finest Department of Manpower and Immigration in the world. We now have the best system in the world for retraining industrial workers. We have departments of government which assist in finding the jobs and training workers for new jobs when the jobs they held are abolished. This is what we have done to cure the problem of unemployment. We have established the department of regional development so that in areas of economic trouble efforts will be made to start new industries. This program is related to the provision of employment in our depressed areas. It does not apply only in the isolated context of bringing in one industry to create jobs; it applies to a whole area. We are trying to develop not just one industry but a community spirit, and housing projects to go with it. The important thing is to arrive at agreement with respect to urban renewal projects. I am sure this problem will be dealt with by the federal-provincial conference.
I should now like to say a few words on natoinal unity in the context of regional development. We have heard a great deal of half-baked, uninformed criticism in this respect,
June 12, 1969

which as usual has failed to impress the house because it has been unconstructive. I urge the government to establish a national pollution control board in co-operation with the provinces. 1 believe now is the time to develop this idea, because we are embarking upon a course of pollution control which should march hand-in-glove with regional development.	\
It is imperative that new industries be compelled to use anti-pollution equipment and methods as plants and machinery are installed in new areas. Second, as this country opens up and develops in the northern regions, let us not repeat errors of the past by ignoring pollution control. Now is the ideal time to introduce pollution control methods in connection with regional planning and other matters. We should now institute a system of pollution control in the north, and not attempt to deal with the problem when it becomes greater, as is the case now in the southern parts of this country. In fact, if the federal government created a pollution control agency which would lay down for provinces and municipalities standards, ideas and methods of dealing with the problem, Canada would be advancing in the direction of success in the battle of survival and the war against pollution. I have a little more to say on that subject at this time.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
I have participated in the review of foreign policy in the Committee on External Affairs. Today we visited the NORAD centre at North Bay. It is apparent that not only are we well prepared for a bomber attack but that our forces are working in harmony with United States officers and other ranks. I was impressed by the efficiency and preparedness of our fine service officers and other ranks at North Bay.
I believe that our review of foreign policy should include the problem of disarmament and nuclear testing at the same time as the problems of military defence. Surely, members of parliament should participate more in the process of policy development. We have made a good start in this area, but I believe that the External Affairs Committee should be closely involved in the current disarmament negotiations at Geneva. We should know what is going on there and be briefed on it.
In the field of national unity I wish to report on a parade that I witnessed last week which would warm the heart of the toughest minded person. We saw thousands of young 29180-637
The Budget-Mr. Gibson Canadians carrying Canadian flags and singing "O, Canada" as we watched their happy faces pass before us. We were watching the new spirit of Canada, a spirit which has no prejudice but which has a longing to live in contentment, in peace and happiness. I speak of the flag day at Stoney Creek last week when, in the presence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) and of the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Sullivan), we were fortunate to see an example of citizenry organizing a national effort toward national unity. The Kinsmen's club of Stoney Creek organized a large parade in which groups of all sorts of people participated in a gigantic effort to display the national spirit. Somehow I believe that we caught the message from these children. In part it said: "Change your foreign policy; struggle and succeed with multilateral disarmament; strive for a land of energy and devotion to duty through the United Nations-and if you do, this world will be a far better planet on which all of us can live in harmony."
With regard to external affairs, I am proud of this government's policy, a policy of questioning historic practices, a policy of reshaping our goals in this modern world, and a policy which recognizes the vital factor in our lives, namely the necessity for communication, communication with new entities, new people, and new ideas. As the spirit of Canada develops, as I was privileged to see it develop in the presence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I suggest that nothing can stop this country from progressing and developing to become the greatest country that has ever existed.
I urge the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) to pronounce Canada flag day soon. We seem to have slowed down in exhibiting the true spirit of Canada, that is we are not leading the people sufficiently by a symbolic reference to our flag by proclaiming Canada flag day. As was demonstrated last week, we can provide the Canadian people with a sort of identity. Also I ask: What has happened to our national anthem? Why have we not celebrated D-Day recently on Parliament Hill? I do not advocate a complete holiday every year to celebrate D-Day, but I submit that when the Canadian army landed in France it was an historic event and a milestone in the history of freedom. At that time Canadians from many units, both English and French speaking, forged a link in the chain of democracy. I say that there is a place on Parliament Hill and a time to recognize that event and
June 12, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis other significant events in Canadian history. I say that we should commemorate that great day by a tattoo of bands on Parliament Hill and we should inject into that celebration the enthusiasm of young Canadians who really do know the words of the Canada song. We can remove the cannons and replace them with modern words, but we should look back to that historic day with pride and joy.
Furthermore, I endorse the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart) that we place a Canadian flag in the chamber of the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the house, and especially hon. members opposite, will no doubt recall the number of questions that I put to the government with regard to the Devco corporation. Hon. members will also recall the delight they felt when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) found it necessary to read out a telegram from the local union back home telling me to cool down and be quiet-in essence to shut up with respect to my representations concerning the retirement plan. The only problem is that when the Prime Minister reminded the house of what the union told me, neither he nor the government realized that the attitude of the miners in Cape Breton had been reversed. Many representations were being made to me asking me to continue my fight against the early retirement plan proposed to the government. Hon. members opposite will probably find it hard to believe, but last Sunday I found it necessary to stand before a meeting in my home town at which a considerable number of miners were present and tell them that the members of the House of Commons cannot be faulted. I even apologized for the Liberal members in this house because, as I said, this house is not responsible for the plan.
I think this is a case of the tail wagging the dog. I ask hon. members present, and especially the minister present, to pay some attention to my arguments and to examine what is developing with respect to this plan so that a fair deal may be given to the retiring miners. An early retirement plan was brought about by Bill C-135 with respect to the Cape Breton coal miners. The intention was that the mines be phased out over a period of years which would mean a saving to the federal government of upward of $20 million annually, a sum which was paid out by way of subventions and which permitted the coal mining

operation to be carried out over the last number of years.
If I were to discuss pensions, and time does not permit me to do this, I could refer to a great number of subventions granted by the government. The fact that subventions to the coal industry have been cut down, and an early retirement plan made available, might make you wonder why coal miners in Cape Breton have deserved this kind of treatment. They do not deserve this kind of treatment any more than any other segment of the economy which depends on subsidies from the government.
I can well imagine what the situation would be if subventions or subsidies were withdrawn from the agricultural field or if the couple of million dollars which were made available to dig the hole in the ground for the Arts center were withdrawn. It is going to be subsidized to the tune of a couple of million dollars a year. We could have the withdrawal of a subvention in the form of a write-off which was just given to the city of Montreal to the tune of $125 million, or of a subsidy which will be made available across the river in Hull amounting to $200 million. I could go on and on. This is why I say that miners in Cape Breton are entitled to this subsidy, but at the moment the tail is certainly wagging the dog. If the government took a good close look, as I have suggested before, at a public meeting, it would be discovered that members of this House of Commons do not want to associate themselves with what Devco is doing. I feel sure of that, so sure that I am ready to stand up and defend the Liberals, which I have done. This statement can be checked. I am sure that no member of parliament wants to associate himself with the dishonest approach of those who are running this Crown corporation.
Why do I call this approach dishonest? I can give many reasons. The preamble of the bill which set up this corporation recommends closure "unless a substantial capital investment is made" for the rehabilitation and modernization of these coal mines. Farther on, the preamble reads:
-the major coal producer in the Sydney coalfield and reorganize and operate the mines with a view to the rationalization of coal production therefrom and a progressive withdrawal of the corporation-
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
As I say, time does not permit me to go into the full details but I should like to illustrate what I mean by a dishonest approach. If
June 12, 1969

hon. members want to defend their own integrity, I would ask them to read Bill C-135 and also get a copy of the early retirement leave plan wherein, in the second paragraph on page 1, they will read these words:
It is the intention of the corporation to reduce coal mining employment as quickly as possible.
That was not the intent of the legislation.
I say the approach was dishonest also because on page 3 of the early retirement leave plan, a copy of which is given to those who are about to retire, appears this statement in paragraph 3:
Those on leave retain C.P.P. entitlement, and are free to take alternative employment, with half monthly outside earnings over $50 applied to reduce benefits.
In other words, people who are about to retire are given the privilege of earning an extra $50. If they earn over $50 they split it with Devco and the money is applied to reduce benefits.
There was the same dishonest approach used when men were given notice that their services would no longer be required, even though some had put in 50 years with the company. Sent out with the notice of retirement or the notice of dismissal, about which I will have something to say later, was a brochure. Included in the brochure were questions and answers provided by the company so that the employees would know what to do ahead of time. I ask hon. members to keep in mind that there was held out to the miners who were retiring the promise of outside earnings. Question 28 deals, in essence, with these outside earnings and reads as follows:
If a participant in the plan is offered work by Canada Manpower, what does he do?
This is the answer that is provided by the company.
Regarding the potential employment background in Cape Breton, prospects of such a position is unlikely.
So, the situation is this: Having held out a promise to the miners in the over-all plan that was submitted to the government, the company then turns around to these men and says that the possibility of employment is absolutely out of the question in Cape Breton. No one can substantiate this better than the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen), who knows the employment situation on the east coast.
I submit that was a dishonest approach. It was an illegal approach, and it remained illegal until I told the government on April 15 29180-6372
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis that it had not properly looked after the mechanics of the legislation. Following upon that, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) indicated that perhaps the company could recall the letters it had sent out and the notices that informed the men their services were no longer required. I ask, Mr. Speaker, who else but Devco could provide such an answer? Who else but a company run by a man called Fullerton, who speaks to anybody and everybody with the exception of the miners? He has yet to go to the Cape Breton miners and talk to them.
Mr. Fullerton also took a dishonest approach when he appeared before the committee. I questioned him about this matter in the committee and he denied my statements. I say 'he showed contempt of this parliament and I suggest that the government take a look at this political "hanger-oner". That is what he was when the previous administration was in office and he still is. He has more to say about free love and sex in Sweden, about which he writes in local newspapers. This is the man who is trying to tell Cape Bretoners how to live and what to do with their lives. This is the man who questions truth in the committee, as I can show from the evidence.
I should like to mention another situation that occurred in this regard. A Mr. Black-more, who was formerly president of the coal board in the U.K., visited Canada, bringing with him the reputation of being a closer of coal mines. He submitted to t'he government a scheme that went even further than the government's own proposed legislation. I would ask the members of the house, in the name of justice, to read through Bill C-135 and the early retirement leave plan provided by the government, as well as the notices sent out to the miners who were forced into retirement. They will then see the promise that was held out on the one hand and denied on the other.
When I tried to make some representations on behalf of these miners, the president of the United Mineworkers Union suggested that I should keep my mouth shut. But what is the situation today, Mr. Speaker? I would ask anybody who is interested to read the correspondence, clippings and telegrams in this connection, all of which indicate that the stand I took on behalf of the miners was the right one, namely that these men were forced into early retirement. At a meeting I attended last Sunday afternoon I stated that the members of this house would not associate themselves with such a move. I ask members
June 12, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis on the other side of the house to examine the evidence and to tell their own government to take another look at what Mr. Fullerton and his company are doing, because they are certainly not being just in this just society.
When the plan was first announced the president of the U.M.W. criticized it as going too far too soon. He also criticized the idea of opening up a new mine at Lingan. He did not believe a new mine at Lingan should be opened because it would be at the expense of other collieries. Although the union had nothing at all to do with drawing up the plan, for some strange reason Mr. Marsh, the president of the union, along with Mr. Fullerton, sees it as a great boon to the coal mining industry. He stated that opening a new mine at Lingan would usher in a new era for the coal mining industry in Cape Breton. Last Sunday afternoon, Mr. Speaker, the highest paid executive officer of the union stated that the opening of a new mine at Lingan would mean closing down all the other collieries. So, there we have a difference of opinion between two union officials.
In alleging there has been a dishonest approach I would also call into question the use of the Unemployment Insurance Commission fund. I have been trying to get answers from the government in this connection. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) indicated to me, in all fairness-and in this respect I have no criticism of the U.I.C.; I want that clearly understood-that when the men applied for U.I.C. benefits, the U.I.C. did exactly what they were supposed to do. But the over-all approach of Devco is dishonest because they are now using the U.I.C. fund to pay the pension that was held out to these men.
Let me give an example of what I mean. A retired miner who is married and has, say, other dependents can receive a top pension of $3,000 a year. The U.I.C. could be providing that man in his first year of retirement with $2,760 of his $3,000. As I have previously stated, if this retired miner makes extra earnings he has to turn back half of any amount over $50 to Devco. In fact, he could hand over to Devco more than he gets from Devco. I agree it is applied to reduce benefits, but this is not what the U.I.C. was intended for.
If these men had been able to remain on the job until they reached the full retiring age, then they would have been entitled to whatever pensions they had earned plus their U.I.C. benefit. As I have said before, this would have given them somewhere in the

vicinity of $2,600 to $2,800 a year in U.I.C. payments. Some of these men have paid into the fund for as long as 29 years and it is their money. This money belongs to those who contributed to the U.I.C. fund over the years. Certainly, it does not belong to the Crown corporation to do with it what it wishes.
I say the action of the Crown corporation is illegal, because I hold in my hand a letter written to an individual requiring him to reimburse the U.I.C. a sum of money because he had left a particular job voluntarily. This is the sort of thing that is going on now in Cape Breton. I have told hon. members what is going on in Cape Breton. These men who retire at ages of between 55 and 60 are being paid pensions. Altogether, they receive $250 a month. Of that amount $230 comes from the U.I.C. and $20 from Devco, that big, generous corporation headed by Mr. Fullerton who seems to know more about free love in Sweden than about the workings of a coal mine or coal miners. At one time coal mining was considered an essential industry in this country and the miners have every right to expect just treatment. So important was coal mining during the last war that miners who wanted to join the army, navy or air force were told, "No you cannot join the armed forces and serve your country. You must stay in the coal mines and perform an essential function".
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Some may say that I am repeating myself. Well, Mr. Fullerton should remember that the miners were promised something. He may make all the speeches he wants to make. I don't care. If hon. members opposite tell their minister that Devco is falling down on the job, there is hope the situation may be corrected. What else can be done? The U.I.C. funds are being used in the promotion of this scheme, and all the promises to our miners are being forgotten. Miners are being forced to retire before they want to. I have spoken in the house before on this matter. Miners are entitled to work until proper retirement age. There is no justification for retiring them early against their wishes. I only ask for justice. I only ask hon. members to bring this matter to the attention of the minister.
Written agreements between the unions involved and the former company indicate that the retirement age of miners is to be 65. For some reason or other some of those miners who have been forced out have retained copies of the letter signed by Mr. Orr, the president of Devco, and co-signed by
June 12, 1969

Mr. Clubb, the then president of Dosco, in which it is indicated that working conditions for miners will remain the same under Devco. Now, Fullerton and company want to break that agreement. They are trying to tell the Canadian people and these miners that the agreement meant nothing because the provision respecting early retirement is now contained in legislation and that legislation supersedes the general agreement. In essence, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Fullerton is making a liar of the minister. And the minister indicated on or about January 15 that the agreement would be honoured. He said that agreements existing at the time of the take-over would be honoured. I cannot cite the page number of Hansard which shows that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion gave that undertaking but if hon. members wish to see those remarks I will look them up. In any event, I can provide them with a copy of the letter to which I have alluded.
As I say, there is a letter from Mr. Orr, the president of Devco, and co-signed by the then president of Dosco, in which the men are told that their working conditions will remain the same under Devco. Clearly, those conditions are not the same, because Mr. Fullerton and company argue that the provisions of the new law supersede the previous agreements. That is nonsense and I do not think any court in the land would uphold such a claim. After all, it can be argued that the Devco people violated the agreement in the first place. I repeat, the minister said in this house on January 15 that existing agreements would be honoured. He also said that notices sent to men being forced off their jobs could easily be recalled. It was precisely at this point that Devco said it was under no binding legal obligation to give one month's notice to the men. Notice was only being sent as a courtesy. What nonsense is this? How can Douglas Fullerton and company say to a man who has worked in the mines for 40 years, "This is a courtesy letter only."
I ask the government to examine Bill C-135. Better still, why does it not look at the Donald report. Look at the recommendations of that report and then look at Bill C-135. I ask the government to look at the early retirement plan. I hate to say this, but in this case we have the tail wagging the dog. I do not often defend Liberals, but I defended Liberal colleagues on Sunday afternoon when I said that I did not think any member of this house would wish to associate himself with
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan the kind of injustice being perpetrated against our Cape Breton miners.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I bring this matter to the attention of the minister, Mr. Speaker, in the hope that the miners of Cape Breton will obtain justice and that Mr. Fullerton may get the just boot.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take advantage of your customary latitude in the budget debate in order to add a few words to the debate of last Thursday, May 29. On that day the New Democratic Party moved the following motion for the house to consider:
That this house condemns the failure of the government to provide policies to prevent further takeovers of Canadian resources, industry and financial institutions by foreign corporations, thus increasing the danger of foreign domination of Canada's economy and culture to the point where Canada's political independence is threatened.
The N.D.P. considered that motion urgent. My reaction to the motion, frankly, was one of disappointment in the N.D.P. I have never been a member of that party but, I assure you, I take great pride, as all Canadians do, in its existence. I admire its dedicated leaders. Although they seek, as do other political parties, the power to form a government, I submit they have had no reason to regret their constant role in opposition. Perhaps they are reconciled to the fact that they will never form a federal government. Nevertheless they can take pride and are fully entitled to do so in their contribution to much that is good in modern society.
Foreign ownership, Mr. Speaker, is an issue of enormous importance to Canada. That issues poses a challenge to government and calls for responses which, I must say, have not yet been forthcoming from the government. Obviously, the government must broaden its dialogue with interested Canadians if it is to develop a proper response to this question. Frankly, I do not know what that response should be. I do not pretend that I can offer an answer. Nevertheless, I wish to take a few ideas and throw them in the air, so to speak, for discussion. What surprises me is that the N.D.P., which likes to call itself the party of the future, has pulled out the old cliehed responses to the dangers of foreign take-overs.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What about Walter Gordon? What did he say?

June 12, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am coming to Walter
Gordon.
This approach of the N.D.P. ignores the value of foreign capital, foreign initiative and foreign know-how which has done so much to uplift the economy and raise economic standards of living in Canada. The living standards of many who support the N.D.P. have been raised by this foreign capital. Of course, I am speaking of the working man.
The N.D.P. has not proposed, just as Walter Gordon did not propose, any solution which would give us the maximum benefits that flow from foreign ownership, from foreign genius and capital while preventing at the same time the threat of foreign dominion. Perhaps the N.D.P. has not been able to think of an answer to this question. I have not been able to think of an answer. Frankly, I think the problem is a difficult one. What the N.D.P. ought to have done in its motion was ask us to discuss the whole problem. That party should have refrained from merely proposing for discussion a worn-out cliche which will cause us much damage in terms of lost capital.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the Watkins report about? Does it not discuss questions of that kind?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, those of us in political life do not know how long we will survive as members of the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You will find out.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
One does not know how long one will survive in the house, least of all as a Liberal member. I say that, because the Liberal party has few doctrinaire supporters prepared to support the Liberal party if it gives lousy government to this country. I discovered during the last election campaign that the opposition parties, especially the Conservatives and the N.D.P., enjoy a certain amount of support from those who adopt doctrinaire, mindless viewpoints. Those parties enjoy considerable unthinking support The Liberal party has fewer supporters of that kind. People elect Liberal members because they think that Liberal members will provide this country with good government. I would also like to think, Mr. Speaker, that if I ever become dissatisfied with this government or the party to which I belong, I will be able to cross the floor of the house. This presents problems.

[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I have studied economics, so I cannot join the Creditistes. I accept the need for positive change, so I cannot join the Conservatives- perhaps they would not take me, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh yes, we would take you.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The New Democratic Party was one place I could go, but they are now beginning to give out the old cliche answers.
Let us look for a moment at the answer proposed by the N.D.P. to the foreign ownership question, the proposal that we close the door. Other countries have done it, some successfully and some unsuccesfully. One thing that is undeniable is that at the margin of decision-making such a policy reduces the flow of foreign capital and talent into the country concerned. If foreigners are to be disadvantaged and deprived of the fruits of their labour, they are less likely to come here. The economic activity which they generate, positively affects the standard of living of Canadians, whether or not they take their profits home. We should, therefore, not seek to keep out foreign capital, but to encourage it.
This proposition is obvious, but I want to take a moment to press it home. People like to say that Canada is a country of untold riches because we have vast resources which we have not yet tapped. Such a point of view is entirely wrong. Untapped riches are not wealth. They do not add to the gross national product or to the standard of living of our poorest citizens, which is the proper test of the national wealth of a society which purports to be a just one. The wealth of a country is a function of the amount of its capital. By that I do not mean resources, but command over resources.
Canada, unfortunately, is a capital-intensive country and will always be one. We will always require more capital for each of our citizens, to provide the standard of living we do than any other country. The reason for this is our demographic dispersion and our harsh climate. To be productive and to be in business we need more miles of road, more miles of railway tracks, more harbours, more buildings and more solid buildings per capita than any other country in the world.
How is this capital to be provided? It is important to realize, and in this debate on foreign ownership it rarely is realized or stated, that all of the capital that is owned by the
June 12, 1969

people of Canada, or virtually all of the capital, is already at work in this economy. If we were to make a decision to buy back that part of the capital working in this country that is owned by foreigners, how would we pay for it? The capital that we have is already at work in our economy.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) referred to the Royal Securities takeover. This is a company apparently owned by Canadians which is being bought by United States interests1. From that concrete illustration it should be realized that the owners of Royal Securities will likely invest the proceeds of their sale in Canada. The total amount of capital in this country owned by Canadians will not be affected by the transaction. The net result of this will not be to decrease the amount of capital in this country owned by Canadians.
I would like to deal with two points made by the hon. member for York South. One of his arguments really supports, the other side of his case. He said, as recorded, at page 9221 of Hansard:
I warn the Canadian people through this parliament that the trend which I have described and which everyone regrets will not be reversed if the economy is left to the control of private corporations. To them a buck is a buck and they will not permit considerations of nationhood to stand in the way of any development even if it moves in the direction of greater and greater control from the outside.
This statement disproves the whole thesis. The hon. member does not complain of foreign ownership, he complains of private ownership. There is much truth in his assertion that corporations, even our best Canadian citizen corporations, are in business to provide goods and jobs and to make money. Surely, this observation cuts across national boundaries. Our Canadian corporate citizens and foreign corporations here are in business to make money. The resolution of the N.D.P. assumes we will find native Canadians thinking more about our national interests' than foreigners. I do not accept this thesis except in a very narrow range of industries. In this respect I agree with the hon. member for York South, but I disagree with the resolution.
Let me move the argument forward. If we are to have corporations act in the national interest, I believe the way to do it is- by legislation. The hon, member for York South said that if the economy is controlled by powerful neighbours our political sovereignty is
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan threatened. This is possible, but not necessarily the outcome. It can be avoided, not by shutting the door to foreign ownership as they propose and losing the benefit of foreign capital, but by appropriate control.
One of the colleagues of the hon. member for York South has outgrown the old idea that foreign ownership, as such, is what should be cut off. I am referring to the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman). He feels that political power, not economic power, is the ultimate authority. This is obvious because, at the extreme, political power can always appropriate economic power through expropriation, Economic strength should not be considered as a means to political sovereignty. One might even say the huge United States investment in this country can be regarded as a hostage, a hostage we can use to enact the political policies we consider to be in the best interests of this country. Considering the interesting research being done in this area by the hon. member for Waterloo, I am surprised his party has picked the old chestnut solution, the easy solution, the one that in the end reduces opportunity in Canada.
I am glad to report that foreign ownership is a problem being discussed by members on this side of the house as well. It is and should be a major issue in Canada, but we have not yet reached the conclusion, and I hope we never do, that there is no alternative, but to shut the door.
I regret the N.D.P., which has so often led the way, is not doing so any longer. The hon. member for York South referred to the Watkins Report. He said the government has allowed it to collect dust.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would, but I might run over my 20 minutes. The hon. member can ask the indulgence of the house when I have completed my remarks.
I would like to read from the Watkins report:
It is a prerequisite to public discussion of government policy and the formulation and implementation of actual policy that more information must be available on the activities of corporations, particularly large corporations, both Canadian owned and foreign owned. Information presently available is generally deficient, and in some respect grossly so, for meeting the three distinct purposes for which the information is needed: public disclosure, economic analysis and governmental surveillance of firms.

June 12. 1969
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan
This first step or requirement has finally been taken and, I agree, it is about time. I congratulate the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) for bringing forward this legislation on corporate disclosure.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
In the few minutes that I have left, Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on some budgetary matters. I have followed this debate with interest, and though not too much of it dealt with the budget there has been great criticism of government for its irresponsibility, for its deficiencies, for its grandiose spending programs. Admitting that the present inflationary situation is a severe one, I would like to introduce into this debate some statistics of interest. These figures are from the International Statistics Service of the World Bank.
Some 27 countries are compared, including most of the free economy industrial countries, as to the amount of inflation, that is, as to the change in the cost of living from 1958 to November, 1966, over an eight year period. These figures show that over the eight year period Canada is second only to the United States in controlling its price levels. In that eight year period U.S. prices increased 14 per cent, and Canadian 16 per cent. In Germany, whose economy is often praised for its stability, prices increased 22 per cent. In the United Kingdom, which is a socialist country, the increase was 27 per cent. In Sweden, much admired by many, the increase was 34 per cent, and in Japan, the land of the modern economic miracle, the increase was 50 per cent. Inflation is no laughing matter. Indeed it is our most serious national problem. The point I want to make is that it is a serious international problem, and our government stands up well in comparison with other governments in its dealings to control inflation.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, and using the latitude permitted in this debate, I would like to tell a tale of two cities. There have been allegations made in this house in the past few days that Montreal is Canada's favourite son, and that Toronto is less favoured. These allegations have even come from this side of the house. The Toronto press has picked up the cause, and these matters are being projected as a cause celebre. Mr. Speaker, such allegations are without foundation.
I have spent the day reviewing figures and checking the financial contributions of the federal government to each of these cities. I

would like to read to you the results of my findings, and I think what I have found will indicate to you that Toronto has not been less favoured than Montreal in financial terms. But before I read the figures I would like to say one thing. I do not believe any government should be judged on the old porkbarrel basis. I do not think it matters, or should matter, how much the members for a particular part of the country are able to bring home to their constituents or riding from the federal treasury. I would rather judge a government on whether it has or has not provided justice in our society. My expectation and my hope is that this government on this basis will earn the support of my city in the next election.
Here are the figures. They make rather dull reading. I compare apples and oranges in many ways. In some items, there are different periods compared, but for each item the period is the same for both cities. In some cases I have matched loan against loan rather than grant against grant, but I am being consistent in dealing with these figures in that way.
First, Expo-Montreal got $159 million for Expo, including Habitat; Toronto got nothing. In public works Montreal got $11,100,000; Toronto $12,500,000. In harbours Montreal got $185 million, again more; and Toronto $25 million. In airports Montreal got $31 million; Toronto $25 million. Centennial projects other than Expo-Montreal zero; Toronto $3 million. Municipal development projects, that is loans to cities, and grants-Montreal $40,500,000; Toronto $54,800,000. In winter works programs Montreal $2,200,000; Toronto $4 million. Conservation authority, water conservation projects-Montreal zero; Toronto $9 million. In housing, Mr. Speaker, Montreal $477 million; Toronto over $1 billion. In the total Montreal got $905,800,000, and Toronto $1,133,300,000, a difference in Toronto's favour of $227,500,000. But, as I have said, Mr. Speaker, these figures mean less to me than they seem to mean to many, and than they seem to mean to the Toronto press. When one checks these figures one finds Montreal is by no means a favourite son.
May I say, with respect to federal participation in the life of our city, that it tends to be submerged. It is below the surface. It is in projects that are shared-cost projects, in projects that are presented as provincial projects, but in many of these provincial projects the federal contribution is as high as 85 per cent and even 95 per cent. This is where Toronto has obtained the advantage over Montreal.
June 12, 1969

I deeply wish there were a federal presence in our city. I would like it very much if there were an impressive head office, a federal building on an enormous scale in our city. I would very much like to be able to point to something-

speechtext:

I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to this four day debate on the subject of the budget which was brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) last week. I was interested to note that a great many members expressed their dissatisfaction with the unsatisfactory economic conditions which prevail in urban Canada. Most of the other members who took part in the debate expressed their dissatisfaction with the highly unsatisfactory conditions that exist in rural Canada. The only reaction I have been able to ascertain on the part of the government is that it takes the view that the economic situation in Canadian cities, so far as the ordinary citizen is concerned, is serious but not hopeless, and that the economic situation in rural Canada is hopeless but not serious.
I say this because there seems to be no sensitivity whatsoever on the part of the government to the very severe economic conditions under which many parts of rural Canada are living. Whether you go to western Canada where there are vast quantities of unsold wheat and low quotas, or to the Maritimes where for the third year there are unsatisfactory prices for potatoes and many other products, or whether you look at the agricultural situation in central Canada, you have to come to the same conclusion that the rural economy is suffering because the primary producer is being caught in a cost-price squeeze.
I am not suggesting that members of the government are not conscious of their responsibility, but I see very little evidence of the government's ability to make an accurate diagnosis of the malaise affecting the Canadian economy and how it should be treated. Instead I find that several ministers whose departments in the general sense might be termed economic ones such as Trade and Commerce, Finance, Area Development and so on, each have their favoured nostrum, each have their favoured cure for what ails the Canadian economy. They rush about, one in one department introducing legislation 29180-638

The Budget-Mr. MacLean which will cost the taxpayers a great deal of money and another in some other department insisting that the defence expenditures, for example, be cut. Then, someone else will have some other suggestion. Each one is determined that he has the cure. This strikes me as being very similar to the situation in respect of a group of quack doctors who were visited by a patient for the treatment of a disease the cure for which they did not know. I have the highest respect for the medical profession today, but if one goes back far enough in history one will find situations which bear a striking resemblance to the performance of this government.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
In this regard the other day I happened to look up the history of the last illness of a famous lady, the Marchioness of Douglas, who passed away in 1674. The best doctors in the land were obtained to look after her. The first doctor who saw her on January 15 applied a plaster to her navel at a cost of 16 shillings. Then, she was forced to take orally two drams of oil of amber. The following day she was given an enema. The patient still got worse so another specialist was called in. This treatment went on for days until eventually one day the unfortunate lady was given a dose of hysteric and purging pills, two blisters for the ear, a suppository, and seven ounces of a cordial and anti-hysteric julep. She still got worse. So, the final expert was called in. He prescribed some more medicine and ended up when she still continued to sink by bleeding her. The total cost of the treatment was something in the order of 467 pounds, 14 shillings and fourpence. There is a striking similarity between the activities of this government, which Canadian taxpayers have suffered in the last number of years, and this sort of thing. The saddest part of it all is that it is the patient, or victim perhaps I should say, who pays the bill.
There are some economic facts of life. I am not one who thinks the question of economics has yet become a science. I believe there is a great deal of research work which should be done by governments, if not by anyone else, to determine the effect of certain policies and the causes of certain economic illnesses so that they can be treated with a reasonable degree of objectivity and a reasonable certainty that the treatment will be effective. I am no expert, but it would seem to me we must get down to some basic and serious economic facts of life. One of these is that we cannot
June 12, 1969

The Budget-Mr. MacLean live beyond our means without having to pay the bill in the end.
I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance for his proposal to balance the budget. I hope this can be done. I do not agree with his methods entirely because I think with the tax load under which the Canadian people are staggering at the present time should be sufficient to produce a surplus of at least $1 billion if the savings were made which could be made. I know this is difficult. At this point in time it may be impossible because for the last number of years in parliament here we have been passing what I believe has been ill conceived legislation. Everyone came in with his favourite piece of legislation which he thought would serve to make him an honest man because of something he said in a previous election campaign or on some other occasion. The result has been that it has been necessary to amend or repeal much of this legislation or replace it with something else. This is all very costly because it means that boards are set up which employ a large number of experts and civil servants. This all costs a great deal.
The only way in which the Minister of Finance found it possible to balance a budget was to prolong a tax burden that is bearing very heavily on the Canadian people. At the present time the levels of taxation are not acceptable. They should be reduced. I believe that we have too much government in the federal sense. From 1950 to 1968 the ratio of civil servants to population has gone from 1 in 106 to 1 in 87. I have nothing against the civil service. I think we have an excellent civil service so far as it goes, but I am not so naive as to think that if some of a thing is good more of it is better. I think that one person in 87 working for the federal government is too high a proportion. As a nation I do not think we are getting full value for all these extra civil servants. It is no fault of theirs, but they are assigned to tasks which are unproductive or not sufficiently productive to benefit the Canadian people. Concurrently with this increase, the average income tax paid per Canadian has increased from $89 to $264 per annum.
The costs of government generally have gone up astronomically. Federal government expenditures from 1962 to the present have increased from about $7.5 billion to about $12 billion. The cost of carrying the national debt due to inflation and high interest rates has gone up at an even greater rate. The cost of carrying the debt of *11 levels of government

in Canada has gone up since 1963 from $1.4 billion to $2.2 billion. The total cost of government has increased from about $13 billion to $23 billion if you take all levels of govern^ ment. The personal debt situation is not any better. Because of the high level of taxation in the nation in the last calendar year, Canadians increased their personal debt by about $1 billion. They have to pay high interest rates which siphon off some of their purchasing power. I believe this situation is partly due to the age in which we live in which a politician can be speaking on television with a whole battery of soap salesmen telling him what to say.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
This is not an atmosphere from which good government evolves. I think we hit an all time low during the compaign before the last election when the successful party seemed to adopt the strategy, in some cases at least, that the federal election was not something equivalent to the selling of soap, but equivalent to the selling of Indian snake oil. You have to keep the minds of the people as far away from the issues as possible. I think this was the feeling of the government. It had to do this for fear it might not be returned. The government bragged that it had going for it a mania. I would not boast about being in power because of a lot of maniacs around.

speechtext: What did we promise in expenditures?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You promised many things, including the just society.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But what did we promise in expenditure?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That involves a matter of opinion. I do not think the great number of Canadians who live below the poverty line would agree with you.
I realize that my time has almost expired. I did wish to refer to another subject but there is not time so I shall leave it. I do wish to say, however, that this is a time when all Canadians-and I have great faith in the future of our country providing we act intelligently, maturely, sensibly and look carefully at the situation before we decide what to do-have a very great responsibility along with members of the government and opposition parties to make sure we are not guitly of mistakes for which our children and our children's children will be paying for decades, perhaps generations.
June 12, 1969

Let me say that it might be well for us to recall one of the most widely read books of its time, "The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire". It sets forth five basic reasons why that civilization withered and died. These were the undermining of the dignity and sanctity of the home, which is the basis for human society; higher and higher taxes and the spending of public money for free bread and circuses for the populace-the Roman empire collapsed under a load of tax, but I would not imagine the Roman empire could have footed the bill of the C.B.C. for more than about three months-the mad craze for pleasure; sports becoming every year more exciting, more brutal, more immoral; the building of great armaments when the real enemy was within, and the decay of individual responsibility.

speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I question the legality of the vote we have just completed. It was my understanding that hon. members on this side of the house indicated the motion would be carried on division. That is to say, I understood that an hon. member on this side would say "On division" when Your Honour proposed the motion, and that no formal vote would be taken. With that understanding several hon. members left the chamber only to be surprised when outside the chamber by the ringing of the bells.
